CHANGE OF AFFILIATION-MEMBER FOR VERDUN-ST. PAUL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this morning is a very momentous and trying occasion for me, worse than a divorce.
For the past several days, Quebeckers have been awaiting a response from the member for Verdun-St. Paul and I feel I must deal in an open, honest and forthright manner with my colleagues from the Conservative Party, with my colleagues in Opposition and, above all, with the House of Commons.
Therefore, I have asked to rise on a question of privilege to read a brief statement which will reveal to all my reasons for embarking on a new course.
For more than five years, I have had the honour of representing the riding of Verdun-St. Paul as a member of this government. It has been a pleasure and a true honour for me to serve my fellow citizens. It was also a great pleasure for me to work with the Prime Minister of Canada, the Right Hon. Brian Mulroney. However, my personal principles and convictions compel me to take a stronger stand and to differ with some of the major issues of the day, notably the Meech Lake Accord.
Henceforth, I intend to participate fully in the debate surrounding this Accord since Quebec's future is involved. I cannot remain silent on this important issue since I would be unable to face my children if they approached me in several years' time and said: "Father, you were there; you said nothing, you did nothing". It is
not by muzzling the members of the governing party that we will find an adequate solution to the problem.
The recently tabled Charest report proposes, in my opinion, other amendments to the Meech Lake Accord. As a Quebecker, I find these amendments unacceptable and I continue to believe and to maintain that the original Accord must be observed and upheld.
Mr. Speaker, it is clear that Quebec constitutes a distinct society and this has been the case since the early days of confederation. Moreover, I still do not understand why this committee was set up. I contend that we must uphold the agreement as it was originally drafted by the First Ministers at Meech Lake.
Therefore, out of respect for the party that I represent here in the House, and because I disagree with its policy prohibiting members from commenting on the current situation, I consider it my moral obligation to resign from this government, and to continue fulfillment the mandate the voters of Verdun-Saint-Paul have given me. Therefore, as of today, I will sit as an independent member.
I would also like to point out, Mr. Speaker, that I still consider the Prime Minister to be a trustworthy, honest person since he has made every possible effort to ensure that the integral nature of the Meech Lake Accord is upheld.
I want to assure my constituents from Verdun-Saint-Paul that I will continue to represent them and to serve them to the best of my knowledge and ability. The 1,200 members of our local association know that I have always favoured the Quebec option.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak the words that have been playing at the back of my mind for months now: Mr. Levesque, you were right after all. Thank you.

COMMENTS OF MEMBER FOR BEAVER RIVER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising in response to a point of privilege raised by the member for Calgary West on Friday, May 18.
I would like to make several short points in order to respond to the hon. member for Calgary West. I do appreciate that the hon. member followed proper procedure on Friday by informing my office shortly after 9 a.m. before raising the question after 12 noon. Of course, last
Thursday he raised a similar question and, although he did not give the Speaker the required one-hour notice and he had to be reminded by the Speaker to put the appropriate motion, I was willing to respond immediately to the experienced member's concern.
Although my state of mind, my mens rea, I believe is the legal term, did not intend to cast aspersions on the hon. member, I saw, on reflection, how my remarks could be incorrectly interpreted so I immediately rectified the situation.
Now, some seven weeks after that original comment in the House, the hon. member says there is a question of privilege.
On page 8430 of Hansard the hon. Transport minister, then Justice Minister and government House leader, said about me:
I guess I have to say that a lot of hours go into this job from everybody. Being a member of Parliament means that you are on top of what is going on in this House while the House is open and sitting. If you cannot be there yourself then you have party people who keep you advised of what is happening and what your responsibilities are. If you do not want to go through your party official you can always ask the Thble.
Mr. Speaker, that statement was made with regard to me and I think the hon. House leader's sage remarks are read and certainly understood.
I am the only member of my party in the House and my staff and I try to keep track of everything that goes on in the House. If the hon. member cannot rely on his party officials' competence or ability to keep him informed, then it is up to him, certainly, to read Hansard himself or have his staff review it for him. If the hon. member feels overworked perhaps he ought to lighten his workload so that he is able to keep up with what is going on in the House as well.
This brings me to citation 82 in Beauchesne's Fifth Edition at page 25 which reads:
A question of privilege must be brought to the attention of the House at the first possible opportunity. Even a gap of a few days may invalidate the claim for precedence in the House.
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that the awareness of a single member, many weeks after the original statement, does not meet the time requirement for a question of privilege in this House.
Also, I do note that there were several other members of the member's own party in the House at the time of my statement on April 5. Had they believed there to be a
May 22, 1990

question of privilege it would have surely been brought up immediately at the time.
The Merriam Webster Dictionary says of the words bribe, bribed or bribery: "to corrupt or influence (one in a position of trust) by favours or gifts, something offered or given in bribe". As a teacher by profession, Mr. Speaker, I tend to rely on dictionary definitions, unlike lawyers who use the Criminal Code.
As no member rose to raise a question of privilege before now, I believe the majority of members took my words and meaning at the dictionary value and did not take it that I meant any legal definition to my words. I was using my statement to reflect an aspect of Parliament perceived by Canadians and which, I believe, is in need of reform.
As this House knows, I was elected as a member of the Reform Party of Canada. The Reform Party believes in, stands for and speaks about constitutional reform and parliamentary reform. We believe in the message of reform and in fundamental reform to Parliament, this institution, to make the elected representatives more responsive to the wishes of their constituents, and we do not believe this institution functions perfectly.
I do not believe this is contempt of Parliament but rather a necessary expression of the views of many Canadians in a democracy and a fundamental, absolute privilege granted all members of Parliament to function effectively in a democratic society. I will not be stifled or intimidated into criticizing practices which I, and many other Canadians, view as morally reprehensible.
I must stand on the meaning which I intended to deliver which was that there are presently in the parliamentary system rules, practices, customs and laws which are designed to serve the political parties for which MPs are elected and the Monarch's Governor General's Privy Council rather than serving the constituents who elected them, unfortunately.
I meant to say that if promises of rewards are used to garner support from wavering MPs, such as favours or patronage appointments and positions, while not constitutionally or statutorily illegal, certainly looked upon badly by the public. I meant to draw attention that day to the need for parliamentary reform and the need to make this House a place where constituents' views are expressed, not just party views.
Routine Proceedings
I am not in contempt of Parliament, Mr. Speaker, I am only a messenger of public contempt of practices of patronage that undermine trust in our democratic institutions. It is not time to condemn me as a messenger. It is time to set up a royal commission empowered to examine all parliamentary practices.

Mr. Speaker, when I rose last Thursday it was on the basis of an editorial. I agree with the member that the issue at that point in terms of that editorial was closed. I subsequently discovered that the comments had been made in the House. The motivation that I had last Thursday was to rise

because of what the editorial said about my personal behaviour.
On reading Hansard of April 5 and the phrase "we know that other members are being bribed to vote for the GST or risk losing precious lifetime pensions" it is obvious, I think to anyone who is a student of the Criminal Code of Canada, Section 119, that an accusation of bribery is a very serious offence.
In terms of Section 41 of the Parliament of Canada Act, a member is prohibited from receiving any compensation whether "directly or indirectly, for services rendered or to be rendered" in relation to any "matter before the Senate or the House of Commons or a committee of either House". A member who contravenes this section is liable to a fine of $500 to $2,000 and for five years after conviction of that offence is "disqualified from being a member of the House of Commons and from holding any office in the Public Service of Canada".
I rise on the question of privilege on behalf of all members because there is an opportunity in this Chamber. All a member who feels that any member of this place has behaved inappropriately, has indeed been bribed and has succumbed to that bribe has to do is rise in his or her place and name the member and ask for the matter to be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.
Otherwise, we are all tarred with the brush of unspecified members. If the member believes that any member of this Chamber has been bribed, he or she should simply rise and make the charge. I did that in relation to the behaviour of two of my colleagues voting twice in the Chamber some weeks ago.
An hon. member puts his own reputation on the line by naming members, but one cannot leave all members of this Chamber accused of being bribed and succumbing to the bribe. It is simply inappropriate. Mr. Speaker, if you find that there is a question of privilege, I would be happy to move the usual motion.

He said: Mr. Speaker, this is the beginning of a debate that will last for two days. It is not a partisan debate perhaps, but a debate involving members of Parliament of various stripes who are dealing with a very profound issue, an issue involving life itself.
That being said, I move this motion to change the sentencing provisions from two years to 20 years to reflect on the severity of the crime involved. What we are talking about here in this amendment is to amend the bill which right now has a term not exceeding two years-and I read from the bill-as the sentencing for contravening the new proposed Section 287 of the Criminal Code.
This bill is a bill to outlaw abortion. It has a number of exceptions included in it, but the stated purpose of the bill is the following, and I read from the first lines of Section 287: "Every person who induces an abortion on a female person is guilty of an indictable offence".
That being said, if we are talking about an individual is guilty of an indictable offence and then serves two years imprisonment for contravening that indictable offence, the message we are sending out is that this is a Criminal Code provision, but a Criminal Code provision which is not necessarily very serious.
Mr. Speaker, if you wonder why I make that charge, why I say that a two-year sentence is inappropriate for contravening the abortion law, I want to compare the sentence to other sentences applied in various situations. I will read from the Criminal Code of Canada and I will provide examples to the Chair of various other sentences and the punishment imposed in various cases.
Section 233(1) of the Criminal Code is entitled "Dangerous Operation of Motor Vehicles, Vessels, and Aircraft". That has a penalty of imprisonment for a term not exceeding five years. "Dangerous Operation Causing Bodily Harm", this has a penalty of a term not exceeding 10 years.
Often in the Criminal Code we see the expression used "punishable upon summary conviction". That means, according to my colleagues who are learned in the law, that the sentences could be as much as two years less a day; in other words, virtually the same thing as the government's proposed abortion bill.

May 22, 1990
Government Orders
I give an example of bills that have as a punishment a summary conviction. Section 234(1) of the Criminal Code: "Failure To Keep Watch On Person Towed". If someone is being towed behind a boat, the penalty for failing to watch that person is summary conviction; in other words, potentially two years less a day. The "Towing of Person After Dark" section reads:
(2) Every one who operates a vessel while towing a person on any water skis, surf board, water sled or other object during the period from one hour after sunset to sunrise is guilty of an offence punishable on summary conviction.
Towing someone on water skis after dark has virtually the same penalty attached to it as contravening the abortion law, the taking of a human life.
The Law Reform Commission of Canada prepared a report entitled Crimes Against the Foetus some time ago. While I do not agree with everything in the report, I do support to a degree the comments made by Mr. Joseph Maingot, Q.C., former Law Clerk of Parliament, who said about laws generally the following:
The law does not exist for the sole or primary purpose of punishing illicit acts. It exists, as an expression, in a broad sense, of the kind of people we are. It does not merely regulate our behaviour, it articulates and symbolizes our values and beliefs.
If that law symbolizes our values and beliefs, would it not also be true that the penalty attached to it would reflect the value we place on human life? When the penalty for committing an offence related to that law is two years, the same as towing someone on water skis by boat in the dark, then I submit we are not serious in adopting a law if we do not increase the penalty provisions that go along with it. For this law to have teeth, not only in terms of its enforcement but in terms of what it symbolizes, surely the sentencing should be 20 years, not two years. The penalty would then fit the crime of the destruction of a human life.

Mr. Don Boudria (Glengarry-Prescott-Russell)
moves:
Motion No. 22
That Bill C-43 be amended in Clause 1 by striking out line 16 at page 2 and substituting the following:
"twenty years".
Mr. Speaker, I shall be very brief with regard to this amendment. As a matter of fact, this amendment is similar to the first one inasmuch as the penalty in the first motion is the same as in the second: obviously if contravening section 287 of the Criminal Code makes one liable to imprisonment for 20 years, it seems to me that the penalty for an infraction of the proposed section 288 of the Criminal Code should be the same.
Perhaps I should point out for your benefit, Mr. Speaker, and for that of all Canadians, that section 288 would punish everyone, and I quote the bill:
- who unlawfully supplies or procures a drug or other noxious thing or an instrument or thing, knowing that it is intended to be used or employed to induce an abortion on a female person.
Section 288, Mr. Speaker, refers to what our ancestors called a pessary. Therefore, if it is wrong to induce an abortion in a mechanical manner, if you will, using a medical means in the case of section 287, and if such action is to make a person liable to a maximum sentence of 20 years, it seems to me that the same penalty should apply for providing a pessary or a drug to a woman in order to induce an abortion and therefore, obviously, to end the life of the unborn child.
This having been said, Mr. Speaker, I would ask you and all my colleagues in this House to support the two amendments I have just moved.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I wish that the procedure were somewhat different this morning because I end up making my speeches one after the other and do not have the opportunity to hear comments from my colleagues. I invite those comments. I know we will have a full debate later but, nevertheless, debates in the House are always far more productive when a large number of members participate. That being said, I do not fault the process because it is better than what could have happened in a situation whereby we could have started for instance debating the first amendment and virtually spoken of

Government Orders
nothing else for two days. We could have eventually voted on amendments that had not been discussed in this Etouse.
The process may not be perfect but it is better than the alternative could have been so I do not want to be critical of those who have proposed the form that we have before us.
Dealing with the amendment in question, regardless of what side of the abortion issue one is on, surely one would recognize that this is a serious issue. It is so serious that in those rare cases where I believe that an abortion should be available surely then it should not be performed by anyone else but a medical doctor.
This motion was seconded by my colleague the hon. member for Winnipeg North who we all know is a medical doctor and a professor of medicine. I think it is particularly symbolic that this professor of medicine, my colleague from Winnnipeg North, agrees with this particular motion.
I think other members should note as well that whether one agrees with me that human life begins at conception, or at some other time prior to birth, the taking of that life involves just that, the taking of human life. If there is a situation that warrants the taking of that life, which I submit is the very rare occassion when the life of the mother is at risk, and I submit that it should be very rare, then surely only a medical practitioner should perform the abortion and not, as the bill proposes, a medical practitioner or someone under the direction of a medical practitioner.

Abortion, Mr. Speaker, is such a serious matter that we would certainly not want anyone but a physician to carry out such a procedure.
I maintain that abortions should be nearly non-existent but, in those rare instances where an abortion is required, surely it should not be performed merely by someone under the direction of a physician but actually by the doctor himself, or herself, as the case may be.
Therefore, I trust that my colleagues, whatever their views on the issue of abortion, whether they agree with me generally or not, will in all conscience agree that abortion is such a serious matter that it should definitely not be performed by anyone but a physician.

However if the amendment does pass, then I would like to wholeheartedly support the legislation.
The issue of abortion is not a new one, certainly. It is not something that we have to wrestle with as a modem society because it has never been dealt with before. It is a debate that has gone on for several millenniums. It is every bit as serious today as it ever was. I know those who disagree with me will invoke so-called "choice", as they have the right. However, I want all colleagues to remember that the choice of one should not be done at the expense of the life of another.
I was reminiscing this weekend. I was reading up on issues involving choice, freedom and liberty, and I was reminded of the United States civil war wherein the Confederates of the south were fighting the north. Young men were giving their lives for liberty, or so they claim. The liberty that they were seeking to preserve was that liberty which enabled them to subjugate someone else's liberty.
Similarly, when we invoke choice, we should remember that what we are saying is that the choice that we are allowed to make, according to those who advocate that point of view, is the choice not to bear a child even if it

May 22, 1990
Government Orders
means the destruction of the unborn child. I cannot agree with that proposition.
As I indicated before in another speech in this House, I do not know where life begins. I think it begins at conception, but I am not sure. I do know that when a child is born there was a child at some point before birth; otherwise, a child would not have been born. It would have been something else. If a child is born, then a child was in the womb. When a pregnant woman loses her life in an automobile accident, we never hear the comment that a woman and her foetus died. It is always: "the woman and her unborn child." The point I am making is that this woman obviously wanted that child. When her life and that of her unborn child are lost, we consider it two lives lost. When someone does not want to bear a child the destruction of it is not seen as the destruction of human life.
The degree to which we want that life seems to make us, as a society, able to make a decision whether life exists or not. Life does not exist because we want it or do not want it to be a life. Life exists because it is there. If that life is there, it is there whether it is wanted or unwanted, or whether parents are wanting or unwanting. It is there regardless of that consideration.
I would submit, Mr. Speaker, that this is probably the most important amendment with which we will be dealing in this debate. Granted, it changes the bill radically, but more important, it gives an opportunity to speak positively on the value and dignity of human life.

speechtext:
Motion No. 12
That Bill C-43 be amended in Clause 1 by striking out line 16 at

He said: Mr. Speaker, as we come down to the final hours of debate on Bill C-43, and we will be debating various amendments today and tomorrow, I do not think it comes as any surprise to members on either side of the House as to where the member for Fraser Valley East stands on this issue. It is an issue that crosses all party lines. It is an issue that is a family matter, an issue that each of us in the House must take very, very seriously.
On December 17, 1986,1 rose in the House to make a statement. At that time I said:
-British Columbia still has the highest abortion rate in the
country, 26 abortions for every 100 live births.
In other words, over 20 per cent of the children conceived in British Columbia are killed by abortion. That is a tragedy.
We are dealing with putting a law back on the books because the law that was on the books has been struck down. This morning I was looking through a book published by the Canadian Automobile Association in conjunction with Reader's Digest. It is entitled: You and the Law. It states in part:
The law under which we live was molded by men who wanted a wide range of individual freedom. But they knew that there must be rules indicating where the freedom of the individual ends and the freedom of others begins. For everybody to be free to use the highway, there must be rules of the road that everybody obeys; without them, the highway becomes a graveyard. The same considerations apply with equal force in many other avenues of life. Seen in this light, law is an instrument of liberation. It is not a series of booby traps cunningly concealed. It is, in large measure, a guide through the maze of human relationships that surround us, many of them strange until we have explored them.
You would not think of taking a journey through a strange country without a map and a guidebook. No one should expect to get through life without trouble unless he has some awareness of what the law permits and requires, and of the ways to conduct himself in the presence of the law.
What the House is endeavouring to do is to set the guidelines as to what we should have on the books with regard to abortion.
I have written to many of my constituents in terms of Bill C-43. In explaining it to them I have said that the bill attempts to address the void in the law that exists as a result of the 1988 Morgentaler decision of the Supreme Court of Canada which found the then law to be in conflict with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Since 1988, Canada has not had a law pertaining to abortion. This situation, I find, is intolerable. As a consequence, we have before us today Bill C-43.
In this bill the government is sending a message to our culture. It is saying to Canadian society, clearly and in no uncertain terms, that the taking of the life of an unborn is unacceptable.

May 22, 1990

This is an objective standard stipulated in the bill. It puts into place a benchmark, an established and acceptable norm. It lets Canadians, specifically the scientific and the the medical communities within Canada, know that this is the standard to which they must adhere.
To ensure that this bill addresses the issue in a realistic and workable manner the bill amends the Criminal Code. This ensures federal jurisdiction throughout all of Canada. The bill incorporates criminal sanctions in the case of violations of Criminal Code provisions.
Finally, the bill protects the life of the unborn from the moment of conception on.
What is often viewed as a major flaw in this bill is the health provision for exceptions to the Criminal Code provision. It is to this end that I am proposing the amendment that stands in my name, to achieve a stricter wording for the health provision.
Bill C-43 places the making of this medical decision in the hands of a woman and her physician. Without the doctor's recommendation an abortion cannot, by law, take place. Medical doctors are the only ones who can actually make the decision. They are the only ones capable of determining whether an exception to this law is valid and necessary.
A few weeks ago a publication was sent to all members of the House by the Citizens for Public Justice. The title of that publication was A Plea for Life and Justice for All. It was dated April 5.
On page 13, it asks the question: "What do doctors really think the abortion law should say?" The answer is taken from an August, 1989 survey done by the Canadian Physicians for Life which sponsored a survey of over 50,000 physicians in Canada. The survey group included all the 43,000 members of the CMA. The response rate of over 20 per cent, or 10,000, is quite large for a single mail-out survey to doctors, especially in the middle of the summer. The number of responses is over six times larger than that from the most recent 1982 CMA survey.
Some of the key responses were:
2/3 of physicians support some form of legal restraint on abortion.
2/3 of physicians find the broad definition of health as an
indication for abortion unacceptable.
Government Orders
2/3 of physicians see the CMA policy as representing abortion on
request, yet only a minority share this position on abortion.
We know that with the tremendous number of abortions-and I have cited what they are in British Columbia-we certainly do need something on our books with regard to abortion. It is not my proposal to deal with this in isolation from other members of the House.
When I was growing up, we heard medical reports concerning people who were in hospital. The major hospitals were not near my home. I lived in a very small community where there was no hospital. The reports would always state that "so and so was on the critical list", "so and so was deemed serious", or "so and so was doing well" and so on. You could get a sense of what was happening.
That is what I am trying to do here. I am trying to send a signal to the medical community for when it deals with the life or the health of a person being threatened and whether the word "seriously" is used in its terminology.
I also want to say that the next motion that will be before us is presented by the member for Kitchener. It states in part:
- the medical practitioner has concluded that there is no other
medically acceptable treatment to alleviate the health risk.
When it comes to the definition of health and the use of the words "physical, mental, and psychological", I am pleased that the amendment of the member for Markham-Whitchurch-Stouffille would delete the word "psychological". It states that the definition of "health" includes, for greater certainty, "physical and mental health".
I suggest to all members of the House when looking at these amendments these three be taken as a package. There are other amendments which each of us will have to consider seriously as to whether or not we should support them and whether the House can support them as a whole.
I would like to quote from another paragraph that was in the report of the Citizens for Public Justice. On page 14, it states:
We live in a broken world. All of us suffer, in one way or another,
from distortions and injustices due to our failure to do justice, show
mercy and walk humbly with God. But all of us still have both the

May 22, 1990
Government Orders
opportunity and the responsibility to be of healing service in our wounded world.
CPJ seeks to do justice to the Supreme Court's conclusion that the right to life of the human foetus may be protected by Parliament. We want also to ensure that alternatives to abortion are available. Women have a right to full information about the alternatives available to them in dealing with pregnancy.
I cannot put it more succinctly than that.

Motion No. 13
That Bill C-43 be amended in Clause 1 by striking out line 16 at page 1 and substituting the following therefor:
"threatened and the medical practitioner has concluded that there is no other medically acceptable treatment to alleviate the health risk."
He said: Mr. Speaker, before beginning my comments with regard to this motion, I would like to commend the member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell on his comments in regard to the amendment that he put forward, Motion No. 10. I would like to say to him I strongly endorse and agree with his amendment. I will be supporting it when we come to it.
I would like to begin my remarks on my amendment by saying that my amendment should not be taken in isolation from two other amendments put forward by my colleagues the members for Fraser Valley East and Markham-Whitchurch-Stouffville.
The three amendments taken together would, first, add the word "seriously" before the word "threatened" on line 16 at page 1.
Second, my amendment would add the words: "and the medical practitioner has concluded that there is no other medically acceptable treatment to alleviate the health risk".
The third amendment would specifically exclude the word "psychological" and, thereby, socioeconomic considerations, from the definition of health on page 1.
Taken together, all three amendments would greatly strengthen Bill C-43. Their total impact would be to make this bill, which is now pro-life in form but prochoice in substance, into a bill which would be pro-life in
both form and substance. The bill, so amended, would then truly balance the right of the mother to the security of the person in Section 7 of the Charter and society's interest in the protection of all human life from conception.
The Supreme Court, in its Morgentaler decision of January, 1988, spoke specifically only to the rights of the mother and not to her unborn child. However, the court clearly invited Parliament to consider the rights of the unborn, as Chief Justice Dickson stated:
Like Beetz and Wilson, I agree that the protection of the foetal interests by Parliament is also a valid government objective. It follows that balancing these interests with the lives and health of women is a major factor and clearly an important government objective.
These three amendments taken together would achieve that objective. The word "seriously" states the obvious. No abortion should be done frivolously or for non-medical considerations. But we all know that many are.
Dr. Morgentaler simply requires the signing of a consent form. This form was filed with the legislative committee on Bill C-43. All it requires is that the patient understand the risks of the operation and that she clearly wants the abortion. Dr. Morgentaler does not ascertain whether that abortion is therapeutically required to save the life or because of severe physical or mental risk to the mother. One just asks, signs a form to show one wants it and understands it, and then gets the abortion.
Second, by specifically excluding the word "psychological" from the definition of health, we are eliminating between 82 per cent and 96 per cent of all abortions. The Canadian Medical Association, when it appeared before the legislative committee, said the following:
It is recognized that 85 per cent to 95 per cent of induced abortions are done for psychiatric reasons, but there are very few absolute psychiatric reasons that are a threat to life, such as severe depression with suicidal risk. Most of these psychiatric reasons are for psychological and social reasons, or humanitarian reasons.
Another group which appeared before the committee was the Canadian Physicians for Life. According to the Canadian Physicians for Life, 96 per cent of abortions are performed for non-medical reasons.
The Badgley report of 1977 indicated that 82 per cent of Canadian physicians surveyed for conditions under
May 22, 1990

which they would support a request for an abortion, could be accounted for by social and economic factors.
U.S. Planned Parenthood states that in 1988, in its experience, 96 per cent of abortions were performed for non-medical reasons.
The National Action Committee on the Status of Women, when it appeared before the legislative committee on Bill C-43 stated:
Women have abortions for many reasons. Most of them are social
and economic in origin.
Third, specifically to my amendment, I would like to say the following. The CMA, Physicians for Life and several other witnesses who appeared before the legislative committee told us that abortion is a medical act. In fact, according to Dr. Lamont of the CMA, abortion is a serious medical act which could even, although rarely, result in death.
From my experience as a hospital board member and the first chairman of the Kitchener-Waterloo Hospital's Risk Management and Quality Assurance Committee, I know that every operation in every hospital involves a tissue analysis or pathological review and is subject to audit procedures to ensure that the medical act performed achieved the minimal risk concerning infections and was truly medically necessary. Yet there is no tissue analysis committee for the aborted child. There is no pathological review. There is no audit as to whether the medical act of abortion was truly necessary. Abortion is a privileged operation done, in the vast majority of cases, for non-therapeutic, non-medical reasons.
Therefore, although my amendment, if proper medical evaluations and procedures were followed would not be necessary, is unfortunately absolutely essential to ensure that they are.
The amendment would require doctors, in forming their opinion as to the necessity for the abortion, to do what they do for every other medical act, that is, determine whether there is any other medically acceptable treatment to alleviate the health risk.
This bill, weak though it is, does not provide for the medical act of abortion for cosmetic surgical reasons. In my opinion it is fundamentally wrong and surely unacceptable medically to use medical intervention to solve or deal with what are essentially, although sometimes
Government Orders
difficult, social problems. Nor should a doctor take out one's tonsils or appendix, or whatever, if there are other means to treat that health risk. Abortion should always and only be performed when there are no other medically acceptable means to treat or alleviate the health risk.
This is the practice in Salvation Army Hospitals, and no one could ever accuse the Salvation Army of a lack of compassion for those carrying an unwanted child. Their position statement given to the abortion committee contains in practice the essence of my amendment. It reads as follows:
The Salvation Army supports efforts to protect and promote the welfare of the weak and defenceless, including the unborn. It takes seriously the rights and needs of both the foetus and the mother. Termination of a pregnancy may be justified in those rare instances where, in the judgment of competent medical and allied staff, the pregnancy poses a serious threat to the life of the mother or could result in serious physical injury to the mother.
Witnesses who supported and recommended the amendment I have put forward are Citizens for Public Justice, the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops and the Evangelical Fellowship of Canada, to name just three.
The Canadian Council of Catholic Bishops in speaking to such an amendment stated:
We are convinced that this amendment is critical to ensure that all therapeutic alternatives are explored and that abortion is not used to remedy other problems or the stress and anxiety that may ordinarily accompany unexpected or undesired pregnancy.
In seeking legal constitutional advice on the constitutionality of the three amendments taken together, I have found that although no one can foretell future decisions of the court with certainty, these three amendments should be constitutionally acceptable. In fact they might even enhance the constitutionality of Bill C-43 by providing greater clarity and certainty as to its definitions and intent.
Therefore, in conclusion, I urge members of this House to support each of these three amendments as well as Motion No. 10 put forward by the member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell.

Motion No 14

May 22, 1990
Government Orders
That Bill C-43 be amended in clause 1 by striking out lines 18 to 20
at page 1.
Mr. Speaker, as you know, Motion Number 10, which was moved earlier, was intended to withdraw the element of health from criteria which would mean, in fact, that abortion would only be allowed when the life of the mother would likely be endangered.
Thus, since health would no longer be a criterion according to Motion no. 10, it goes without saying that Motion no. 14 would simply eliminate the definition of the word "health" included in the bill.
As we all know, the definition of "health" can be misused. My colleague, the member for Kitchener, was making precisely this type of comments earlier. According to him, the definition of "health" should be restricted. As far as I am concerned, it should simply be taken out, as long, of course, as there is agreement on the order relating to Motion no. 10.
To give you an idea of the definition, Mr. Speaker, according to the dictionary, the word "health" has various meanings, but in the bill it includes certain elements.
Let me read to you the definition of "health" given in the bill:
"sante" S'entend notamment de la sante physique, mentale et
psychologique.
At least that is what the French version says. It is a bit equivocal. If you refer to the English text, it says:

"health" includes, for greater certainty, physical, mental and
psychological health;

Therefore, the French text gives a very specific definition of health; but in the English text and, as we all know, both versions have force of law, of course and the word "health" includes the bill and lists everything and does not exclude anything.

"Flealth" can mean physical, mental and psychological, but does not exclude any other definition of health as well. It leads me to believe that health means absolutely anything you want it to mean.

Motion No. 16
May 22, 1990

That Bill C-43 be amended in Clause 1 by striking out line 19 at
page 1 and substituting the following therefor:
"considerations of physical and mental factors as they cause a serious threat to life and".
He said: Mr. Speaker, before I speak to my proposed amendment I would like to indicate to the hon. members for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell, Fraser Valley East and Kitchener that, in essence, the substance of my motion complements theirs. I will be supporting their proposed amendments.
One of the most serious problems evident in Bill C-43 is the vagueness with which "health" is defined. The Supreme Court of Canada in deciding the Morgentaler case indicated that health must be defined clearly.
If you do not define and require at least that the gravity of health must be considered, then it is really vague. Even before that, to include the word "psychological" would in fact allow for such vagueness to be legalized.
The former Minister of Justice stated that "psychological health" included behaviour, emotions and problems of adjustment to the environment. He further stated that the word "psychological" is broad enough to utilize the word "socioeconomic".
Under his interpretation of this bill, and as he stated when he was asked at committee, poverty itself may be a basis for abortion. That will not be acceptable.
Because the word psychological is broad and nebulous, it will give occasion for abuse and would permit abortion for any form of distress.
Moreover, without the amendment that I have proposed, physicians would not have the clear guidance that they ought to have from this piece of legislation. Some physicians may interpret it as allowing abortions if the woman is merely unhappy with or inconvenienced by an unwanted pregnancy.
The bill itself even advances the erroneous idea that abortion can aid a woman's psychological health, for which there is no evidence, medically speaking. As a consequence, there could be a serious adverse effect on the relationship between physician and patient. A woman who desires an abortion, for no medical reasons, could be led not to tell the whole truth about her ailment, about the conditions that truly affect her medically. When that happens, the relationship between
Government Orders
patient and physician becomes threatened. How can a doctor issue a proper diagnosis when the medical history is not full and thorough? How can a physician make a diagnosis when the information that the physician is receiving is clouded?
With such a loose definition of health, the foetus, the unborn is not protected at all. In fact, we may ask the question, why Bill C-43? The reason we are proposing a bill against abortion is precisely because we would like to protect another life, or there is no basis for this medical procedure to be in the Criminal Code. To me, the only indication why this medical procedure ought to be in the Criminal Code, in contrast to other medical and surgical procedures, is because this is the only procedure for which, when done unnecessarily, the life of the unborn is truly compromised.
Therefore, if we allow this bill without the amendment that I have proposed, it will result in abortion on demand and the protection of the unborn would be an illusory situation.
Before 1940, almost all indications for abortion were truly medically therapeutic. By 1950, many so-called psychiatric reasons accounted for more than 50 per cent of all abortions. Currently, 90 per cent of all abortions are performed on the basis of so-called psychiatric disorders. But the degree with which these disorders are assessed, whether they truly threaten the life or the health of the mother, is certainly subject to question.
In summary, I have proposed the amendment that we consider physical and mental factors, and in a sense deleting the word "psychological", because that will be included in "mental", but with the understanding on the part of the medical profession that the degree of mental disturbance ought to be severe and that this severity of disturbance would seriously threaten the life and health of the patient.
That is the essence of my proposed amendment.
I wish to quote the first two principles from the 1990 edition of the Code of Ethics of the Canadian Medical Association. First, consider the well-being of the patient. As I have indicated, when a physician approaches a pregnant woman as a patient, that physician automatically has two patients, the woman herself and the unborn she is carrying. The second principle is, honour your profession and its traditions. It has been the tradition of medicine that the physician protects all his patients in

May 22, 1990
Government Orders
this instance, both the pregnant woman and the unborn child in her womb.

speakeroldname: Mr. Francis G. LeBIanc (Cape Breton Highlands - Canso) moved:
speechtext:
Motion No. 17A
That Bill C-43 be amended in Clause 1 by striking out line 19 at
page 1 and substituting the following therefor:
"physical and mental".
He said: Mr. Speaker, before addressing my own amendment to Bill C-43,1 would like to compliment my friend and colleague, the member for Winnipeg North, for his diligent work on the legislative committee studying Bill C-43. As a medical doctor, he has added an important element to the committee's deliberations. I also want to compliment him on the eloquent and persuasive manner in which he spoke in support of his amendment, Motion No. 16. I want to say at the outset that I fully support his amendment even though its passage will make a vote on my own unnecessaiy.
I would also like to associate myself with the amendments proposed by my colleagues, the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell, as well as the member for Kitchener, and the member for Fraser Valley East who spoke earlier.
Motion No. 17A, a motion which I have proposed, seeks to limit and strengthen the definition of "health" in Clause 2 of Bill C-43 by removing "psychological" as a relevant category of health that would make abortion legal under this legislation. I have proposed this restriction for three main reasons.
First, in my view, the inclusion of psychological health as a relevant consideration for procuring an abortion, in particular as the term has been used in the explanatory notes to the legislation, and in the words of the former Minister of Justice, virtually sanctions abortion on demand.
In fact, I submit that it would be worse than abortion on demand. If no reasonable medical grounds can be found to justify the procedure-which, if we are honest with ourselves, is the case in all but the rarest of circumstances-women would then have to describe the psychological trauma, real or imagined, that carrying the baby to term might produce.
In the naturally stressful situation of an unwanted pregnancy, for whatever reason, the law would provide no support for passing through the early anxieties to what may be a far different frame of mind, if the option to carry the pregnancy to term was chosen.
The law would allow the psychological consideration to justify an easy way out.
This is not to deny that real socioeconomic or health factors may be at the root of these concerns. The woman may be facing the prospect of single parenthood on a low income. She may be a teenager. The new arrival may provoke a confronting and bewildering adjustment to her lifestyle and to that of her family. These are real situations. They deserve the support and compassion of society. They call for programs and policies that get at the root of these situations, not for the panacea of abortion, of snuffing out the life of an unborn child.
A second reason for proposing this amendment relates to cases where foetuses are found to be physically deformed, underdeveloped, or mentally handicapped. Modern methods of ultrasound technology now make it possible to identify these cases at early stages of pregnancy. Naturally, a woman who faces the prospect of giving birth to a handicapped or deformed child would be anxious to have this cup pass her by.
Physically and mentally disadvantaged children, whether arising from birth or accident, impose new costs on society. Yet, in a deeper sense, they add an important richness to our society, to the humanity which we all share, as those who have worked with or been privileged to be associated with celebrated cases of persons suffering from these handicaps will only too readily testify. This richness is in peril if we permit, as the psychological reference in Bill C-43 would permit, abortions for so-called eugenic considerations.
A childhood friend, Mary MacLennan, who was bom with no arms, with the support of her family and community has gone on to become a successful lawyer, said this before the committee on Bill C-43: "If this is the way that those who are making the laws are thinking and this is what is being used to influence people, then I think those with a disability, whether you are born with one or whether you acquire one when you walk out that
May 22, 1990

door and try to cross the street, I think you have to be very concerned about creating a mentality like that".
Finally, I reject the claim made in defence of the psychological provision that the Supreme Court decision in the Morgentaler case makes this a necessary part of any abortion legislation. The government's background notes to Bill C-43 state on page 6 that "based on the majority reasons for judgment in the Morgentaler case, permitting an abortion if the psychological health of the woman is threatened, is constitutionally required".
I believe that this statement is a serious misreading of the words of the Supreme Court decision.
The Chief Justice in the Morgentaler decision blames the delays caused by abortion committees and the lack of a definition of health for the psychological threat to a woman's security of person. He states: "The psychological injury caused by delay in obtaining abortions, much of which must be attributed to the procedures set out in Section 251, constitutes an additional infringement of the right of the security of the person".
Further, he adds: "There is increased psychological stress imposed upon women who are forced to wait for abortions, and that this stress is compounded by the uncertainty of whether or not a therapeutic abortion committee will actually grant approval".
Nowhere does the decision state that the absence of a psychological health consideration is a breach of security of person.
Bill C-43, amended by Motion No. 17A, sufficiently eliminates these delays. There are no procedural delays and there is a more precise definition of health. In fact, by providing a more precise definition of health, by saying up front what will and will not be accepted as grounds for abortions, and by grounding these conditions in an honest and rigorous application of medical science, abortion legislation is enhancing the security of the person, of the unborn child and of the expectant mother. It will foster a responsible attitude in both women and men toward their sexual behaviour.
The wishy-washy inclusion of psychological health in this loose clause of Bill C-43 plays to the weakness in us all. It invites us to invent reasons to use to extricate ourselves from difficulties which, had the easy options
Government Orders
not been so readily available, we may have chosen to avoid.
For these reasons, the health definition is one of the most glaring weaknesses of this legislation which would need to be strengthened before Bill C-43 could enjoy my support. My motion is an attempt to do that.

Motion No 17B
That Bill C-43 be amended in Clause 1 by striking out line 19 at page 1 and substituting the following therefor:
"physical and mental health, and does not include psychological".
He said: Mr. Speaker, as a pro-life person, I am disappointed in Bill C-43 as it now stands. It is not restrictive enough. Therefore, I wish to put forth an amendment which would delete the word "psychological" from the definition of health.
In its brief to the committee the Canadian Medical Association stated: "It is recognized that 85 per cent to 95 per cent of induced abortions are done for psychiatric reasons, but there are veiy few absolute psychiatric reasons that are a threat to life such as severe depression with suicidal risk. Most of these psychiatric reasons are for psychological and social reasons or humanitarian reasons".
I want to make the point that my amendment is part of a group of three pro-life amendments put forth by my colleagues from Fraser Valley East, British Columbia and Kitchener, Ontario. I would also like to associate myself with Motion No. 10 standing in the name of the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell.
The Right Hon. Prime Minister of Canada, when speaking in opposition to the capital punishment debate on June 22, 1987, made the following statement:
All of us share in the tragedy and sorrow of the taking of a human life, whether criminally inspired or from anger or passion -It is wrong to take life, and I can think of no circumstance excepting self-defence to justify it.
The act of abortion is clearly the taking of a life. The abortion issue is the most important issue this thirty-fourth Parliament will deal with. While many people contend that Bill C-43 accommodates all views, it certainly does not satisfy my pro-life position. Virtually all pro-life people I have spoken with believe that the bill is weak and flawed. That is why this package of amendments is needed in order to protect the unborn

May 22, 1990
Government Orders
human foetus. Canada has been without abortion legislation now for over two years. I believe legislation is urgently required in order to protect the unborn.
In their brief the Citizens for Public Justice make this statement in the introduction: "The abortion issue probes the values of our nation. It is messy, complicated, and explosive. Most people wish it would just go away. But this issue cannot go away. What we decide to do with it will tell us something fundamental about who we are and what we value. Therefore, evading the abortion issue is as much a decision as any action we may take".
Then they go on to state; "Our national response to this challenge will show what kind of people we are, what kind of future we seek both for our children and our grandchildren, and for Canadian women who must make agonizing decisions".
My wife Sandy and I have shared two personal experiences in our lives which profoundly affect our views on abortion: that abortion only be performed when the mother's life is at risk or in certain circumstances involving rape or incest.
I believe the choice of adoption should be considered by any woman who is considering an abortion. Many couples would love the opportunity to raise a little boy or girl. Sandy and I decided to adopt a baby boy in 1968. We had a family of one son, Howard, and two daughters, Pamela and Leslie, at the time. We believed we could provide a new young son with a warm family life.
So in the summer of 1968 we adopted John Fraser Attewell who was 11 months old at the time. His natural mother had one other baby and was unable financially to raise another child. Fraser will be 22 years old this August. He is married and he and his wife Robin have a young son, William Cody Attewell.
Sandy and I have often thought that if an abortion had been easy to obtain 20 years ago, we may not have had Fraser as a son.
There are thousands of parents in Canada who hope and pray for the loving opportunity to adopt a son or daughter.
As members of Parliament, it is up to us to provide legislation which will protect the unborn. It is up to us to fight for their lives. Thank God we had doctors and nurses who fought for the life of our granddaughter, Heather Attewell.
A little over two years ago, our son Howard and his wife Linda were excitedly awaiting the birth of their first child. Unfortunately complications developed. Heather was born two months premature and weighed only two and one-half pounds. It was then discovered that Heather could not swallow because her oesophagus was not connected to her stomach. Heather spent the first six months of her life in Sick Children's Hospital under the loving care of many professionals. Heather is now two years old. Most of her food is still fed to her through a tube in her stomach, but she is learning to swallow. She is beginning to talk now and she has a baby brother, Derek Attewell.
Hundreds of people were praying for Heather's survival when she was first born. Our prayers were answered. Heather had many people praying and fighting for her life. The doctors and nurses and other assistants were splendid in their professional and caring treatment. We were fighting for Heather's life.
I do not know how many members here have held a two and one-half pound baby. I have, and you see how vulnerable and dependent they are. But let us think of an unborn child, how totally vulnerable and totally dependent they are on us. We as parliamentarians have a grave responsibility to fight for the lives of all unborn children. We can help do this by passing appropriate legislation.
In their brief Citizens for Public Justice recognizes the fact that abortion is the tragic result of a society which does not sufficiently support women, children and families. Therefore, while life protecting legislation is needed, such legislation is not enough. I quote from the brief: "Social policy needs to address many of the factors which lead women to seek abortions".
The brief continues: "CPJ calls upon the federal government to extend its co-operation with the provincial governments to implement an even more comprehensive social policy that addresses factors which lead women to seek abortions, such as prevention of unintended pregnancies, better access to counselling, provi-
May 22, 1990

sion of a full range of adoption options, housing initiatives, and so on. The above list is intended only to introduce areas of concern".
In closing, I sincerely hope and pray that the proposed pro-life amendments will be passed in order to strengthen more adequately Bill C-43 in order to protect the lives of the unborn.

Motion No. 19
That Bill C-43 be amended in Clause 1 by striking out line 3 at
page 2 and substituting the following therefor:
"medical profession, developed from a solid body of scientific knowledge."
He said: Mr. Speaker, again before I proceed to speak to this proposed amendment, I would like to add my voice of support for the amendments advanced by the member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso who spoke so eloquently on his proposed amendment and the member for Markham-Whitchurch-Stouffville.
My proposed amendment in essence emphasizes the need to ensure that the medical opinion shall be based only on a solid body of scientific knowledge and not on a popular opinion obtained by survey polls. The medical standards ought not to be variable, not varying from province to province, not based on fad and fashion, but in fact based on scientific knowledge.
It is necessary to emphasize this point because when diagnosing a woman who is seeking an abortion, a physician may be more preoccupied with the transient, immediate distress of the woman and less with the long-term health of that particular woman. When a physician is guided by popular opinion and not by true scientific knowledge, a physician may do more harm than good to his or her patient.
When physicians allow themselves to be swayed by popular fashion in making critical medical judgments instead of adhering to scientific standards they may not provide the proper medical care. The bottom line is that the physician's decision must be guided by the science of good medicine. Otherwise he or she becomes less of a doctor, only providing a service for a fee, and that is not in the highest standard and tradition of the medical profession.
What some of those who advocate abortion on demand overlook, I submit, is that if pregnancy is to be cosidered as a disease, which it is not, then abortion certainly is not
Government Orders
the therapy either, because we know that after the duration of nine months of pregnancy the whole condition will solve itself.
There are no controlled studies which indicate that abortion is a treatment for normal pregnancy, although the pregnancy may be associated with some emotional and psychological distress.
It is in the tradition of medicine that when a patient sees a physician, first the physician obtains a medical history from the patient, a thorough history of all information relevant to the chief complaint. In this given case, what we would like to be clear is that the physician will continue to adopt the strict science of medicine and ascertain why a woman is asking for an abortion. We know that there can be many reasons including: "I do not like this pregnancy because I cannot afford to support this child after birth", "I do not like this pregnancy because I will not be able to pursue my own professional career", "I do not like this pregnancy because I just do not like it".
The answer to these questions and concerns is not abortion. The answer is counselling, giving the woman true options on how we can help that pregnant woman truly asking for our help go about solving the reasons why she has asked for an abortion.
Next, following the receipt of all the medical information, the physician makes a diagnosis and thereafter considers whether a given treatment approach is indicated or not. It is never the case in medicine that the patient decides "give me this treatment" and the physician follows hook, line and sinker without first getting the medical history, without forming his diagnosis or diagnoses, and without in fact discussing with the patient the alternatives to treatment and management.
When a physician reaches the point of making the treatment plan for his or her patient, then he or she considers whether the treatment approach ought to be medical or surgical. In considering those treatment modalities, the physician also considers the options of treatment-the first, second and third option-and considers the side effects that may emanate from any treatment. This is what I feel this law must enshrine. When a physician forms his or her medical opinion, the physician must be guided and guided only by the science of medicine, by a body of scientific knowledge, and not by popularity, not by fashion, not by fad, and not by a vote during a convention.

May 22, 1990
In this instance I am really saddened that the Canadian Medical Association, of which I am a member, took a vote in one medical convention and then asked how many were in favour of this particular position, without basis whatsoever of scientific knowledge sustaining that. Yet the President of the Canadian Medical Association, before the legislative committee that examined this bill, admitted that medical opinion must be based on scientific knowledge.
Therefore, it is only proper that this House supports my proposed amendments so that we can clarify and enshrine good medical practice. In so doing we will truly ensure the value of this bill and protect the unborn for which this bill has been created.

speechtext:

Mr. Speaker, when I rose in this House on May 11 condemning the desecration of a Jewish cemetery in France, little did I expect that isolated incident to become a terrible pattern of racism and anti-Semitism through ghoulish acts recently in Ottawa and Quebec City. Something is changing in Canada when sick minds feel they must express their political or religious views by defacing tombstones, disturbing graves, violating consecrated ground. Mr. Speaker, in 1940 Canadian National made an agreement with the communities of Colchester County and Truro, Nova Scotia, to provide a highway bridge over the main rail line to Cape Breton in return for the communities giving up and closing off two streets.
For the last several years the residents of the area have seen the bridge disintegrate so much that the weight capacity has been reduced first from 10 tons to seven tons and now from seven tons to five tons. The fact is, the bridge should be condemned.
After years of stalling and delays CN finally agreed in writing on January 18, 1990, to build a new bridge with construction starting in the middle of May. It has not started. The residents of the area need this bridge replaced, with no more excuses, and they are demanding that CN keep with its original obligation made in 1940 and its written commitment made on January 18,1990, to replace this bridge now.

subtopic: TRIBUTE TO PIERRE ASSELIN AND NATHALIE VEZINA
TRIBUTE TO PIERRE ASSELIN AND NATHALIE VEZINA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 14, two young students from my riding who were studying for a bachelor's degree in history and political science at York University in Toronto, left Canada to pursue a course of studies at the University of Hanoi.
This rather unusual destination was chosen following an intensive course in Vietnamese at the South east Asian Studies Summer Institute of the University of Hawaii, during the summer of 1989.
The person who taught the course at the time was so impressed by these young Canadians that he offered to be their tutor in Hanoi.
Pierre Asselin and Nathalie Vezina are the first Quebecers and, in fact, the first Canadians to study in Vietnam.
Mr. Speaker, I invite hon. members to join me in wishing them every success in this adventurous and also quite difficult undertaking.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a Decima research study recently released by the Minister of Employment and Immigration reveals that 66 per cent of Canadians support this government's plan to shift resources from UI benefits to effective job training.
The labour force development strategy is an important and valuable initiative of our government to develop a well trained and diversified workforce that can readily adapt to the challenges of tomorrow. Canadians are aware that without such training programs, Canada will fall behind other competitors in terms of a skilled workforce. This is a realization based on both common sense and economic reality.
Given the evident public support for Bill C-21 and Canada's urgent need to up-grade and enhance training opportunities, it is imperative that the Liberal members of the Senate listen to the Canadian public and pass this bill. Mr. Speaker, Canadians are shocked and disturbed at the news of the desecration of Jewish cemeteries in Quebec and Ontario, the last being in the city of Gloucester. The knocking over of tombstones is cowardly. The painting of Nazi symbols and anti-Semitic slogans is a disgraceful and dastardly act.

Canadians from both official language communities in this country, of different cultures and religions, wish to declare their solidarity with their brothers and sisters in the Jewish community and express their indignation in respect to these racist acts.

doors are opened, your prayer and that felicitous phrase "pour fructifier nos deliberations" and for Canada herself.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to express my feelings of outrage and deep dismay at the desecration of the Ottawa Jewish Community Cemetery in my constituency of Ottawa South last week.
The vandals who perpetrated this crime must be brought to justice under the law. They have brought violence to our community, causing many innocent families both grief and fear, and in the end every one of us has been victimized.
What is equally worrisome is the increase in incidents of hatred and intolerance against Jewish people worldwide. In this century, the world learned a terrible lesson about what can happen when hatred is permitted to overflow into the streets. We cannot indulge in passive acquiescence when this kind of directed racism occurs in our communities or elsewhere.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Prime Minister just said, the Minister of
State (Federal- Provincial Relations) has now met most of our provincial premiers to find out whether it is feasible to call a First ministers' conference. Considering the important reference the Leader of the Opposition made, I may point out that as Prime Minister of Canada, I negotiated the Meech Lake Accord because I absolutely wanted to bring Quebec back into the Canadian family. The Accord does that. I will never agree-I have said so on many occasions, and it has been said by other members on both sides of the House, especially by members from Quebec-I will never agree to let the terms of the Accord be diluted or its objective questioned. We want to ratify the Accord so that Quebec and Quebecers will truly feel they belong to Canada. We have never reneged on our support for the Accord, and we have no intention of repudiating our signature to the Accord. We have always found the Accord acceptable in its present, unamended form, and that position has not changed.
The Charest report proposes a basis for resumption of discussions by the governments to ensure that the Meech Lake Accord is ratified. The report provides the basis. It does not guarantee the results. I have always thought that all members of this House, by unanimously supporting the Charest committee, were telling the parties: We have now found a basis for negotiations. Go ahead and see if you can conclude an agreement, but not at the cost of weakening the Meech Lake Accord. Everyone has said Meech Lake must pass unchanged. That was my position, and I think it is the position of all members of this House.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, the constitutional situation is obviously very serious.
May 22, 1990



Would the Prime Minister not agree, therefore, that the time has come for him to be in direct contact with the provincial premiers to develop a basis for an early First Ministers' Conference which would bring about a satisfactory resolution of the current constitutional impasse?
In other words, certainly the work of Senator Murray is intended to be useful. But does the situation today not require the direct intervention of the Prime Minister on behalf of the House and the people of Canada in contact with the provincial premiers if we want to bring about an early resolution of the current constitutional impasse?

Mr. Speaker, I have been in touch with all provincial premiers; some of them twice, some of them three and four times over the last number of days and throughout the weekend.
These various communications have been actively complemented by a personal visit from Senator Murray who has sought to ascertain the extent to which, pursuant to the committee recommendations, it might be possible for the partners to sit down and to reach an agreement which would resolve the constitutional impasse.
My hon. friend will remember that three years ago, when we signed the Meech Lake Accord, it was not a complicated proposition. All parties in the House agreed and twice voted in favour of a document that was a simple, dignified and straightforward welcome to Quebec back into the Canadian family. That is what we passed, that is what I signed, and that is what I want to have respected.
That having been said, in a three-year time frame, governments changed and the situations changed. What was a simple, straightforward invitation to Quebec to rejoin the family, found itself burdened down with add-ons and some such matters which we were ready to discuss, provided they did not vitiate, in any way, the fundamental provisions of the Meech Lake Accord. I think that was the general view of all members of the committee.
I continue to believe, notwithstanding the difficulties in which we find ourselves, that it is possible for reasonable Canadians to understand quickly and urgent-

ly, the magnificence of the country that we have come to enjoy and love and to make sure that constructive compromises come forward to make sure we keep this nation strong and prosperous forever.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister, who I assume is aware that Mr. Bourassa's cabinet is to meet later today to discuss a common position.
Has the Prime Minister of Canada been in touch with Premier Bourassa to give him the assurance that all three federal political parties in this House are unanimous in their desire to find a solution to the constitutional impasse? And more specifically, will he recall that the members of the Charest committee unanimously reaffirmed their acceptance of Quebec's five demands?

Mr. Speaker, the answer to my hon. friend is yes. I have been in touch fairly regularly with the Quebec premier, the last time being, I believe, yesterday evening. I have always stressed the point that was made and quite properly raised by my hon. friend from Papineau-Saint-Michel. I have told him that the purpose of Meech Lake is to make Quebec a full-fledged partner of our federation, an active partner who would participate fully in the evolution of Canadian federalism. And that is because the Accord will make it possible for Quebecers to feel they are truly part of Canada and want to build their future on that basis.
Yesterday, I noticed one particular comment by Premier Bourassa, which is important in the context mentioned by the hon. member. On the weekend he said, in referring to Canada: "We are one of the most privileged countries in the world. That is why the majority of Quebecers would like to stay and prosper in this country and work together with the country's other groups and other communities".
This statement by the Quebec premier reflects his respect, admiration and deep affection for a united Canada. That is why we negotiated Meech Lake, and that is why we will have to make the following message unanimous: Quebec said yes to Canada, and now it is time for Canada to say yes to Quebec.

Hear, hear.

May 22, 1990

Mr. Speaker, I wish to ask the Prime Minister a supplementary question. Does the Prime Minister realize that it is important for him at this time to play a considerable leadership role in explaining, and not just leave it to the chairman of the parliamentary committee, Mr. Charest, to explain the avenues which this committee explored? Is the Prime Minister himself ready to explain clearly that this report, which was accepted in good faith by opposition members, with the agreement of government members, only explores ways to solve the constitutional impasse and at no time did any of the members of this parliamentary committee want to require 23 concessions from Quebec, that the recommendations and suggestions contained in it are not to be taken as a whole but as a series of recommendations and suggestions to get Canada out of its constitutional impasse and that it is completely wrong to claim that they are 23 amendments, several of which change the essential conditions of the Meech Lake Accord? Is the Prime Minister prepared to defend the thesis that it is part of a compromise and that these suggestions would in no way lead Quebec to amend its five initial demands?
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the right hon. Prime Minister. I certainly agree with the Prime Minister's comments. I think he is saying that all of us in this House have a responsibility for the future of Canada and we take that responsibility seriously.
There is a serious situation in this country and I know that some people are despairing of the situation. But our role is to bring the country together. While we are all concerned about the events of the last few days, we cannot lose sight of the objective, which is to break the constitutional impasse.
I know that the Prime Minister has had Senator Murray speaking to the premiers of the provinces. Can the Prime Minister share with this House what the progress is to date and what specific plans this government has to ensure that we really can break the constitutional impasse?

Mr. Speaker, I must tell you that I am advised that the progress has not been substantial. Unfortunately there are some people-and I say this uncritically-who fail to understand the objective of the Meech Lake Accord.
The Meech Lake Accord was brought about by an agreement in 1986 of the premiers gathered in Edmonton who said that we cannot go on with Quebec not being a willing part of the Constitution and therefore we call upon the federal government to begin negotiations to seek a formula which will allow Quebec to become part of the constitutional deal, willingly, after which we will move to a second round.
There began a process which resulted in Meech Lake. The objective of Meech Lake at the time was not that anyone was seeking to exclude anyone's considerations. The specifically stated objective was that Quebec be
May 22, 1990

brought back into the Canadian family first and that any other matters be dealt with in a second round.
That was a very clear-cut and I think a very noble purpose. We achieved that. That Meech Lake Accord was honourable and, as Jack Pickersgill said, on terms so reasonable they will never come again in our lifetime. That Meech Lake Accord was endorsed twice by the House of Commons.
There were subsequently some add-ons which, in the minds of many Quebecers, have diminished the value of the Accord, and have changed it from its fundamental, noble objective. That is why there is growing frustration in the province of Quebec. They were willing to come on side and to say that by signing the Meech Lake Accord we willingly bind ourselves to Canada, to make Canada whole again, one Canada; we are proud to be Canadians; we sign with enthusiasm the Meech Lake Accord because it binds the nation together.
That is what the Meech Lake Accord is all about. It is now being diverted from that original, very noble purpose. We have to get it back on track so that Canadians understand what it is about. It is about the future of Canada.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Prime Minister. Certainly no one denies what the purpose of the Meech Lake Accord was, and we certainly agree with that purpose. However, I would suggest that, owing to the lack of public consultation and public input, it has gone far beyond that, and this is why the Prime Minister called together a special committee to study a companion resolution.

The unanimous report tabled last week stressed again the importance of upholding Quebec's five principles.

Mr. Speaker, Senator Murray has been seeking common grounds following the recommendations of the Charest report. That is his mission as he is crisscrossing the country. [English]
My hon. friend prefaced her question by referring to a lack of consultation. May I submit to her that perhaps that was not the reason. I do not think that anybody fully understood the implications of the new constitutional provisions in 1982 that provide a three-year period for constitutional amendments to be reviewed.
