Nobody anticipated that premiers would refuse to honour the signatures. I am not quarrelling with the process, I am just saying this was one of the new elements of the 1982 Constitution.
As I say, it was a very clear-cut undertaking by all Canadians which promoted joy across the countiy. I and many people thought that within a matter of months after the signing on June 3, 1987, all of the provinces would have ratified it and it would have passed the House of Commons.
The statement that French Canadians were making was that we want to be part of Canada. You have been asking us for 25 years what Quebec wants, we have just told you. We have acknowledged it, we have a document that is honourable for Canada. It is decent for our citizenship. It is a source of pride for us all. Let us sign it, let us pass it and let us get on with the job of building a better Canada.
That is what we thought would happen. Nobody anticipated that governments would change, signatures would be repudiated, and all of a sudden a very simple, straightforward document of unity would become a catch-all for everybody else's wish list as governments changed across the countiy.
That was not the intention of Meech Lake. That should not be the intention today. We should proceed with the objective of bringing Quebec solidly back into

May 22, 1990

Canada so we will have one powerful country and then go on with these other questions.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, there is certainly no one in this party, and I am sure no one in this House, who does not share the objective and the importance of having Quebec in the Constitution. However, whatever happened over the last three years, whatever misunderstandings or miscalculations there were, we have to deal with what is happening now.
We know that Senator Murray has been consulting with the premiers, that he will do so with Mr. Bourassa tonight and that he has shared some kind of text with them. Every day that that is left unclear, the anxiety over the future of this country increases.
Following Senator Murray's meeting with Premier Bourassa this evening, will the Prime Minister make a commitment to share with this House and with Canadians the exact state of the negotiations, including the contents of the wording? Can he make a commitment to share that with this House and Canadians tomorrow after the negotiations have concluded?

Mr. Speaker, I will be happy to share with my hon. friend and the members of the House any information that is given to me by Senator Murray which I feel could be constructively imparted.
As well, I do have an obligation to consult with very strong and, if I may say, very loyal and courageous supporters of Meech Lake, from the Premier of Nova Scotia to the Premier of Ontario and the Premier of Alberta, people of all political persuasions who have done so much. I plan to keep all people informed including, of course, members of the House of Commons.
I would just observe, in terms of the realities, that what happened really was that a separatist government arrived in 1981 with a shopping list of requests for the federal government which were clearly unacceptable. Most people know that. A federalist government was elected in the province of Quebec in 1985 with a list of five requests, not one of which broke new ground, not
one of which had not been heard of before or debated for years in Canada. I can remember these debates taking place at Laval University 30 years ago on each and every one of those topics. There is nothing new under the sun.
Mr. Bourassa, a Canadian federalist, came forward with a list of five specific requests. They were debated for almost a year and a half. They were negotiated and we had an arrangement. It was clear cut and it did not close the door to the other matters that were raised legitimately for a second round. It was clearly stated in the Meech Lake Accord that there will be a second round and that the first item on the second round will be Senate reform. It was devised with this in mind.
That was the statement by Quebecers and this should never be forgotten. I began hanging around the National Assembly in 1960 and I have watched every Premier of Quebec veiy, very carefully. On June 3, 1987 Premier Bourassa went to the Conference Centre and I want to tell you that it had been a long time since I had heard a premier of the province of Quebec say: "This is a statement of love in Canada. I am proud to be a Canadian. This is a great day for Canada".
That was three years ago and we still have not concluded the deal today. It is time for Canada to say yes to these reasonable conditions of the province of Quebec.

Hear, hear!

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I entered politics late in life, under trying circumstances, but with the best of intentions. Two reasons prompted me to go into the lion's den. The first is the attraction of the beau risque, the worthy risk of co-operating with Mr. Mulroney. The second, Mr. Mulroney himself. In Sept-Iles, on a warm day in August 1984, he made the solemn commitment to bring this country together. I knew as well that he had met this commitment by having all provincial premiers sign the 1987 Accord which would enable Quebec to endorse formally the 1982 patriation.
May 22, 1990

The objective was clear: join the government team to help the Prime Minister obtain the ratification on which the implementation of the Accord was dependent.
It was with some hesitancy that I finally accepted the accord. Indeed, as early as 1982,1 thought that some day English Canada would pay dearly to repair the breach of faith of 1982 and the historical harm done to its own reputation. When I first read the accord I had the impression that Quebec had made light of the fact that it had been humiliated and that it was justifiably indignant. Still, convinced that nothing better could be achieved, I finally concluded that we had to pull ourselves out of the ghetto and prostration where Pierre Trudeau's arrogant deception had confined us. I said to myself that we had to take that opportunity to turn the page on the bitterness of the recent past and, with Brian Mulroney, begin to write a glorious chapter highlighted by acts of faith, tolerant gestures and open dialogues.
Mr. Speaker, there are those who would say that these were mere words and that words do not mean much in politics. But it so happens that I come from a family, a background and a region where words are heart-felt. It is not mere chance if, for instance, the Prime Minister so often uses the word generosity. It is because, basically, he is a generous man.
I also thought that, if anything, the signature of the provincial premiers was sacred. Therefore, I had no reason to suspect that the Meech Lake Accord, bearing the signatures of the Premiers of New Brunswick, Manitoba and Newfoundland, would be dishonoured. There is something deeply shocking in the idea that the very people who chose not to honour the signatures of their predecessors are now trying to make Quebec bear the onus of their own guilt. The sharpest of the three, Mr. McKenna, even reminds me of the wolf that calls out for help to protect the sheepfold it has just ransacked.

speechtext: Now, now, he is not here to defend himself.

All these gentlemen know full well that the negotiations did take place, that the compromises have been made and that Quebec came out of it bloodless after setting the extreme limit of its concessions precisely where proudness loses its meaning.

This is why any request for more concessions is an insult to its sense of honour. The report of the parliamentary committee advocates belittling the distinctiveness of Quebec's society by enshrining, in the same provision, the equality of New Brunswick's English- and French-speaking communities. I also have in mind the still greater dilution of the Accord as a result of the suggestion that the Charter of Rights and Freedoms be jointly applied. And I am concerned about the recommendation aimed at eliminating the unanimity rule to implement Senate reform, and about all the dangers which the ambiguous formula of a "regional approval" mechanism entails for Quebec's veto.
Above all, I consider as altogether unacceptable the recommendation to give Parliament and the federal government the role of promoting and not just preserving the linguistic duality, as stated in the Meech Lake Accord.
That is why I must speak out about the government's strategy to make this report the basis for discussions to call a First Ministers' Conference. I do not doubt Mr. Mulroney's intentions but by conferring this status on the report, the government is, in fact, forming an alliance with the very parties that would impose humiliating terms on Quebec. This report accredits practically every attempt by enemies of Meech Lake to dilute the Accord and deal a fatal blow to Quebec. The report should never have existed. I disapprove of it utterly, and I see no alternative but to leave this government-be it with feelings of pain and anguish-as well as the Conservative caucus, to sit as an independent member.
I implore the Premier of Quebec to avoid falling into the trap that has now been set. I ask him here and now to spare Quebecers one more insult, one more blow to their pride, one more ostracism. I can honestly say that for two years I have constantly supported Mr. Bourassa in his efforts to protect the integrity of the Accord. Today, I say to him that if he refuses to attend a conference where this committee's report will be on the agenda, he will have not only my support but that of all Quebecers, from Montmagny to Rouyn, from Quebec City to Montreal, from Roberval to Baie-Comeau.
I urge Mr. Bourassa to accept as a framework for discussion only the resolution that was passed by the National Assembly in a great move towards unity, a prelude to the new surge of energy that will put Quebec in charge of its own destiny. Let clever politicians, those arsonists disguised as firemen, those sorcerer's appren-

tices, come and tell us here in Ottawa, before the people, before past, present and future generations, whether or not they repudiate signatures that were freely given, at that time of grace in the national life of this country, at sunrise on June 3, 1987.
Mr. Speaker, enough of this hypocrisy! Let the real culprits take off their masks, or if they cannot stand the light of day or fear the judgment that history will pass on them, let them be inspired by Macdonald and Cartier and look to the future, our children's future, and then reach out to the fraternal hand Quebec still offers, perhaps for the last time.
Mr. Speaker, with your leave, in concluding I would like to say to all my colleagues, to the Conservative ministers and members, that it was an honour to serve with them. Ties of solidarity and friendship were forged. I told the Prime Minister in my letter and at our meeting yesterday how much I appreciated him. speechtext: Of course, I well understand that some hon. members would like to speak on the statement made by our hon. colleague, but the Standing Orders do not provide for it. Therefore, we shall resume debate on the order of the day.
The House resumed consideration of Bill C-43, an act respecting abortion, as reported (without amendment) from a legislative committee.

speechtext: We will now move to Motion No. 24.

moved:
Motion No. 24
That Bill C-43 be amended in Clause 1 by striking out lines 5 to 24
at page 1 and lines 1 to 16 at page 2 and substituting the following
therefor:
"code are repealed."
She said: Mr. Speaker, my amendment would turn Bill C-43 into a simple housekeeping bill rather than an act to recriminalize abortion.
Criminalization of abortion is wrong. It does not prevent unwanted pregnancies, which is why women and girls seek abortion. It does not ensure access to abortion services.
This bill is somewhat like making food illegal and then saying that the government will ensure that everyone has access to a grocery store. It makes no sense.
It does not stop legal cases or strike down provincial abortion laws. It seems to create another legal tool to base legal cases on. Provincial laws will not just disappear as a result of this bill, as some would have us believe. As both the Minister of Justice and the Minister of National Health and Welfare are so fond of saying, health is under provincial jurisdiction. The provinces can enact laws regulating medical services at any time they want. These constitutional powers are in no way affected by the presence or absence of a federal criminal law, as constitutional lawyers across this country have told us.
Criminalization does not fill a regulatory vacuum. The Canadian Medical Association and provincial colleges of physicians and surgeons already have guidelines concerning abortion. It is illegal to practise medicine in Canada without a licence.
We have been without a law now since 1988. For more than two years there has been no criminal law on abortion. Criminalization will not make this issue go away. We know that. We have listened to the people on both sides of this issue. It is not an issue in society that is simply going to disappear quietly because there is new criminal law passed.
There will be court challenges. There will be court challenges within a year if this measure passes. All it takes is someone like Barbara Dodd who changed her mind. She could lay an information saying that she knew, and that her doctor knew, that she was not coming in and asking for an abortion because of health reasons.
May 22, 1990

Some pro-choice Tories in this House have turned a blind eye to the ramifications of this bill. They think that hardly anyone is going to be charged, or they have said that it is unlikely that people will be charged, doctors or women.
We do not have criminal laws so that no one will be charged. A criminal law is a serious matter in this country. Henry Morgentaler spent time in jail for breaking the last abortion law. We have heard already from doctors who say that they will openly disobey this law because it is an insulting and a hypocritical law. They say that they will perform abortions because the woman wants one for her own reasons, not for reasons acceptable only to the state.
It is surprising to me to see pro-choice Tories turn a blind eye and to support state control of women's bodies and women's private decisions. The Tories are the ones that go on ad nauseam in this House about privacy, about deregulation, and about as little government control as possible. Yet this is the very same government that wants to dictate to women on their reproductive health.
This bill is wrong. Why do members on the other side feel that they must compromise their values and their principles on this bill?
This is supposed to be, we are told, a free vote. Members did not seem to compromise when it came to the issue of capital punishment.
There is no reason for this bill. The country has operated fine for the last two years without a criminal law on abortion.
The amendment I propose will wipe out the bill leaving only one sentence stating: "Section 287 and 288 of the Criminal Code are repealed". This will have the effect of getting rid of the sections of the Criminal Code that were invalidated by the 1988 criminal court decision in Morgentaler, formerly sections 251 and 252.
If my amendment passes, that will be the whole bill. There will be no recriminalization of abortion.
Anyone in this House who calls themself pro-choice must vote for this amendment. This is the only prochoice amendment proposed to this House. It does not escape notice that all the amendments proposed this morning were proposed by men, and that all of those
Government Orders
amendments would make the legislation even more regressive, even more restrictive to women, than the present bill.
The Liberals and the Tories have proposed only amendments that would make this bill far more restrictive. I know these amendments have come from a minority of Liberals and a minority of Tories.
Thus I appeal to the pro-choice Conservatives and to the pro-choice Liberals in this House to vote for this amendment. Do not let those severe anti-choice amendments stand as your parties' position on reproductive choice.
The amendment I propose is for all pro-choice members in the House of Commons. It is for people in this House who value the integrity of Canadian women and who respect the decisions of Canadian women.
I appeal to all members to put aside whatever party pressures there may be, and vote for this amendment, Motion No. 24. There is a chance for pro-choice members to speak out and show all Canadians that they do have integrity, that they do care about women, that they will vote for their conscience.
I would like to see the Minister of Justice, the Minister responsible for the Status of Women and the Minister of Employment and Immigration vote for this amendment. It is the only pro-choice position. Just because they are being coerced by the Prime Minister and by their paramount commitment to their own political careers to vote against their consciences on the bill, does not mean that they should vote against the amendment.
This is a way out. If this amendment passes, the House will have spoken. The House will have voted against the ineffective approach to the abortion issue for an effective and a compassionate approach.
In this situation criminal legislation is not the answer. Social policy is the answer. Family planning education, research into safe and effective contraception, support for pregnant women and their families are the truly effective approaches to this question.
It is too late now to change peoples' minds about their own philosophical position. It is going to be impossible for me to convince the member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell to vote for my amendment.

May 22, 1990
Government Orders
I appeal to all of you who share my philosophical point of view, who do care about women, who do believe in reproductive freedom, to vote, for the only pro-choice amendment before the House of Commons and cast your ballot for choice. Cast your ballot for the integrity of Canadian women.

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will address some of the points that have been made by the last speaker in the third reading debate.
I rise today in response to the motions put forward for debate at the report stage of Bill C-43, an act respecting abortion.
[Translation\
You already know, Mr. Speaker, that the provisions contained in Bill C-43 are the result of a very long process, of a careful examination of the question, of many consultations and months of study and deliberation to answer this difficult question in the most just and moderate way.

This bill has been carefully drafted to achieve a delicate balance between the conflicting views on the abortion issue.
It complies with the ruling of the Supreme Court of Canada in the Morgentaler case with respect to a woman's constitutional right to security of the person guaranteed in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and to reflect the societal interest in the protection of the foetus.
Clearly, abortion is one of the most divisive issues facing Canadians today.
I am strongly of the opinion that Bill C-43 reflects a balance of the views of the Canadian people in a way that will be acceptable to the majority of Canadians.
It is our role as parliamentarians to bring forward legislation that reasonably reflects the various views and interests of Canadian society in a manner acceptable to that majority of Canadians, and that respects constitutional guarantees.
It is not our role as parliamentarians simply to continue to articulate a particular side of the debate. We must act in the interests of all Canadians.

The highest court in the land recognized this responsibility by stating in the Morgentaler affair that its role was to examine the laws to determine whether the legislative balance of particular interests complies with constitutional guarantees but that it is first and foremost Parliament's task to achieve this balance.
Mr. Speaker, we have taken time and effort to reach an acceptable solution on abortion, in the best interest of Canadians, while respecting and reflecting the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
For many people, it was necessary to seek an accommodation and to recognize that in order to find a basis of agreement on this difficult question, and I emphasize, a basis of agreement that respects differing opinions and constitutional guarantees, we must set aside our personal opinions and act in the interest of Canadians whom we represent.

The legislative committee which examined Bill C-43 and has now presented its report to this House clearly accepted this challenge.
Following months of hearings, including testimony from many individuals and groups expressing strong views at either end of the spectrum of opinion on abortion, the committee recognized its duty to attempt to strike a fair balance between the rights and interests of women and society's concern that the foetus be protected.
The legislative committee has approved Bill C-43 without amendment, and I commend its members for the thoughtful considerations they have given to their examination of the proposed legislation.
As parliamentarians we must assume our responsibilities to bridge the gap created by the divergent views which we and our fellow Canadians hold with respect to the matter of abortion.
Bill C-43 is our best effort at bringing forward a law that will withstand a constitutional challenge. It is a balance that addresses the protection of a woman's security of the person, as identified in the Morgentaler judgment, while providing recognition to society's interest in the protection of the foetus.
May 22, 1990



If we change the bill by accepting any of the proposed amendments in the motions presented, I am quite afraid that the fragile balance we reached in the bill will be broken and that we will pass an unconstitutional law or even go against the objective sought.

The motions to amend Bill C-43 which are before the House reflect the strong divergent views held by the partisans on either side of the abortion debate. Obviously, this law will not satisfy these members. Only absolute positions would do that.
It would be my hope that these members not condemn this bill for not reflecting their own personal positions, but recognize its ability to respond to the concerns of their fellow Canadians in a manner that is understandable, workable and fair.

Without going into the details of each motion before you, I wish to make the following general remarks on the effect of the various proposals to be debated.

You have several motions before you, Mr. Speaker, which, if adopted, would serve to remove or restrict the definition of health or the standard of health required by the proposed legislation, or require exceptional medical circumstances in order for an abortion to be induced.
The imposition of a "serious threat to health" or that a requirement that a woman be in a life-threatening situation in order for an abortion to be performed at any stage in a woman's pregnancy, would be contrary to the reasoning of the Supreme Court of Canada in Morgentaler, and thereby jeopardize the constitutional validity of Bill C-43.
In addition, the definition of "health" in this bill explicitly refers to psychological health in order to comply with the ruling in Morgentaler.
Removal of this ground would, therefore, increase the risk that there would be a successful challenge under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
Increasing the severity of punishment for inducing an abortion outside the exemptions permitted by law from
Government Orders
two to 20 years would have an adverse effect on the constitutionality of the bill, as would attempting to regulate the pre-implantation stage by abortion legislation.

In Bill C-43, we are trying to respect both the judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada in the Morgentaler case and society's interest in protecting the foetus.
Any amendment to the bill that could be perceived as unfairly favouring the state's interest in protecting the foetus to the detriment of the woman's constitutional right to security of the person could endanger the legislation's constitutional validity.

I have policy concerns as well with the motions that would remove the legal protection afforded nurses or other medical staff who assist a doctor in the performance of an abortion or would suggest that a doctor's opinion based on the generally accepted standards of the medical profession would not normally be based on scientific knowledge.
Two of the motions proposed would serve to defeat completely the purpose of Bill C-43-first, by allowing abortions to be induced by any person provided the woman consents; and, second, by repealing the current abortion provisions in the Criminal Code without enacting any replacement.
To suggest that the bill be withdrawn in its entirety does not recognize our responsibility as members of Parliament to bring forward a law that is constitutionally valid and addresses the protection of a woman's security of the person, while providing recognition to society's interest in the protection of the foetus.
I have stated repeatedly that it is our duty to attempt to strike a balance of interests that reflects the various views and interests of our constitutents and respects constitutional guarantees.

I have tremendous respect for the process by which Bill C-43 was drawn up.
Because of the fragile balance achieved in the bill, people of opposing opinions support it.

I believe that it is extremely important to continue to respect the balance that Bill C-43 reflects.
That is why I am afraid that if any of the motions before the House pass, Bill C-43 may not be adopted on third reading.

Any of the proposed amendments, if adopted, would likely upset the political balance sufficiently to alienate support for Bill C-43 from those holding opposing views.

Mr. Speaker, I believe that the abortion issue must be settled by Parliament and not just by the courts.
It is up to us to deal with this issue.
That is why Bill C-43 was presented and why hon. members must support it.

I therefore strongly recommend that we support Bill C-43 by voting against all of the amendments proposed in the motions before this House. In this manner, we will ensure the successful passing of this bill into law.
We will thereby fulfil our responsibilities as parliamentarians in having introduced an abortion law which provides safeguards for Canadian women and reflects society's interest in the protection of the foetus, while at the same time respecting the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

Mr. Speaker, I apologize for not being in the House. Actually I should have spoken before the minister, but I am glad I had a chance to listen to her speech. I would like to say first of all that the Official Opposition has recognized the right of its members to a free vote on this difficult and fundamental issue.
Some very strong views are held on this side as well, and I would also like to take a few minutes, at the report stage of this bill, to explain my own.
Despite the respect just shown by the minister for the process used before the committee that considered this bill, I think we should point out that the committee ignored, and the government ignored and refused to
consider, the tenor of the testimony brought before this committee.
I believe the government decided from the outset that it would refuse to accept any amendments and would reject all testimony to the effect that this is a bill that contains many problems. There are problems with the principle and with the moral perspective. This is not a bill that takes an honest approach to the position it reflects. That is basically what should be said.
I said I have my own position, and it is that the Supreme Court of Canada was right to suggest that first of all, we should respect the right of women to chose freely to have or want to have an abortion.
In this respect, the government's bill does not work because in the framework of this bill, there is no provision for having access to the services of a doctor to have an abortion in the first stages of pregnancy. Before the woman has access to medical services, she must first have the permission of those services. To me, this goes against the judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada.
I have asked the government to make a referral to the Supreme Court of Canada to find out whether the legislation is constitutional. I have my doubts, and practically all the witnesses we heard said the same.
Mr. Speaker, the problem I have with the situation in which we are in now is that pretty soon we will have a ruling by the Supreme Court of Canada on whether or not the bill is legal. Unfortunately, this will happen when we have a pregnant woman who has problems, as in the case of Chantal Daigle and in so many other cases in this country. That is how we are going to determine whether or not this bill is constitutional.
I am very sorry that the government, possibly because of male chauvinist leanings, decided to ignore legal advice and go ahead with some very questionable legislation. In my opinion, in line with the views of the Supreme Court of Canada, in the later stages of pregnancy there are interests respecting the foetus that must be recognized and which we were asked to recognize. Some of the judges of the Supreme Court of Canada expected our committee would hear witnesses that would expound their ideas on the development of a human being that, during pregnancy, becomes a being worthy of legal recognition. And then, in the context of the testimony received, the committee would be able to establish a system that would strike a balance between



May 22, 1990

the very important and legitimate interests of the woman and the emerging interests of the foetus.
This the government refused to do, and the Speaker felt that my amendment to establish this system was out of order. I accept that decision.
As I said, I accept that it was out of order but I regret very much that on the principle, the government did not decide to listen to the witnesses and to create a system recognizing the rights of women, even though some of those witnesses did not want to admit that at a certain point in the pregnancy, other interests come into play but for me-I insist-and for the Supreme Court of Canada, the interests of the foetus deserve to be recognized and protected as much as those of the mother.
Mr. Speaker, we know, as the minister just suggested, that all the amendments before us must be rejected. I deplore it. I will vote against this legislation which neither respects the right to life nor recognizes the rights of women.
Consequently, I personnally think that it is an hypocritical piece of legislation that does not deserve to be adopted by the Parliament of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, this is for me both a duty and a pleasure to debate today in this House this abortion bill. This is a very emotional issue for all hon. members and it forms an integral part of the legal and moral approach of all Canadian men and women in general and my Quebec-Est constituents in particular.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, a great many things were said, a great many opinions were expressed both individually and collectively, and sometimes emotion wins over reason; that is why I felt further thought needed to be given to the matter. Finally, I have come to the realization that, fortunately or not the greater the information gathered from all sources, the harder it became for me to make up my mind.
Yet, Mr. Speaker, I feel I must share with you all the result of this reflection which, in my humble opinion, can only serve to enhance the various sentiments expressed to date. Here are some ideas:
Government Orders
According to Ronald D. Elving, "abortion is now and will remain for many years a politician's nightmare". There is nobody in the House, I believe, who disagrees with this opinion, and it could be said also that this is a societal concern.
Unanimity exists only on two points, namely, that first the abortion issue is highly charged with emotion and second that opinions are highly polarized.
Mr. Speaker, can we reasonably hope to achieve soon a consensus which could make the legislation acceptable to the majority?
I would rather hope so. As Paul Valery wrote: "There always comes a day when a clever man can define in three words the essential of a doctrine which all until then had deemed absolutely incomprehensible".
Of course, I do not think I am such a man, but anybody can seek to hasten the coming of this liberator. The three key elements are perhaps the distinctions on which we should insist.
The first is the basic distinction between the legal and the moral aspects of the matter.
Mr. Speaker, it is always difficult for a layman to view an issue the way the legislator does. Why?
Because when considering an issue, the legislator must keep in mind the good of society, the need to preserve law and order in a society while seeking the common good which dissensions can only jeopardize.
A legislator who is against abortion could vote in favour of a legislation which makes it possible, while not authorizing it, if he felt that it were necessary for the good of society.
A second basic distinction is that between objective and subjective morality.
Objective morality considers things in the abstract dealing with their principles and not their application. It looks at abortion from a general viewpoint without considering the individual case which a real human being confronted with the realities of life has to deal with.
The way a person deals with the abortion issue as such depends on how he or she sees the foetus. There is not much of a consensus on this.

May 22, 1990
Government Orders
For some people the foetus is a part of the mother's body, for others it is just a group of cells, for some it acquires value over time, for others still it is a human being from the moment of conception.
The moral judgment on abortion varies. For some it is as simple as having a tooth pulled, for others it is murder.
Under the strictest moral, meaning Catholic moral, the foetus is a human being from the moment of conception, it has the strict right to live and the state must uphold that right. Therefore it may never be killed directly even to save the mother's life. Under this moral the end never justifies the means. Abortion therefore can never be a means to the best of ends.
We seem to be in an impasse, Mr. Speaker, but when certain Catholic theologians want to apply the official thought to real life, complex as it is in most instances, they do make exceptions by introducing very significant nuances, for these people make a distinction between "doctrinal" and "pastoral" speech. It is not unlike the well-known distinction made by legal experts between principles and their application.
Some of these theologians accept even direct abortion in certain cases, say to save the mother's life, in cases of rape, and others. Others find situations where abortion is the least of two evils. Still others make distinctions: do not allow, but do not penalize; do not allow, but make it possible, and so on.
Even more than moralists, legislators will have to take these compromises into consideration. Above all they will have to take into account the personal conscience that each individual looks upon as the rule which guides one's conduct. Keep in mind that the moral which says one is never allowed to kill a foetus also says one is never allowed to act against one's own conscience. Pro-lifers have no use whatsoever for the subjective moral and the key role which conscience must play in human life.
When legislators are on the verge of passing legislation on abortion they ought not to forget subjective morality. The more numerous the various opinions on this issue, the greater the role of personal conscience. They ought not to forget that there are Canadians who
are not at all convinced that the foetus is a human being or even a living being from the moment of conception, and that destroying it is always a murder.
Mr. Speaker, a major question which my fellow citizens of Quebec-Est often put to me is this: Should the government legislate in this matter? If it did not, the abortion issue would be like so many others which are not covered by law. These problems relate to morals and personal conscience.
Would abortion be more frequent if there were no law? That is a moot point. Apparently the number of murders did not go up after the death penalty was abolished. An abortion is not the kind of operation which a woman is happy to undergo. As the doctors have pointed out in their brief, the procedure is hard on everyone involved. The best protection for the foetus' right to life is built in the human heart by moral values and not by a law, however wise and strict it may be.
So, if Bill C-43 does not pass, it should not be seen as a tragedy.
On what criteria then should the drafting of a law be based in order to be wise will you ask me, Mr. Speaker? I will answer that the wise legislator must remember that he is not a moralist, in spite of his moral convictions. He must not try to impose his personal convictions on everybody through a law. It is hard, however, not to forbid others what one forbids oneself.
The wise legislator must take into account the society for whom he is legislating and the era we live in. In a hundred years from now, things might be different. Our ways may have changed and some of our existing laws may then seem quite inhuman.
The wise legislator must also take into account subjective moral values as well as individual conscience, especially considering we are dealing with a field in which there is no unanimity within a given set of values.
We all know, Mr. Speaker, that not so long ago, the Supreme Court required two conditions to be met for fear of being brought back before the courts and having to go through the whole process all over again.
The first constraint was that it considered section 251 of the Criminal Code to be unconstitutional because women had to go through the too time-consuming
May 22, 1990

process of the therapeutic abortion committee comprised of three doctors who had to give their "consent".
And as for the second constraint, the Chief Justice said that it was unacceptable to force a woman under threat of criminal penalty to carry a foetus to term.
I have heard some people tell me that abortion is nothing more nor less than a medical procedure. But, Mr. Speaker, considering abortion as a medical procedure does not mean that it is not at the same time and more fundamentally a moral act, as is every action taken deliberately or voluntarily and freely. If abortion is a medical procedure, Bill C-43 makes it a crime for anyone but a physician to perform an abortion. That is as it should be.
However, when the Canadian Medical Association maintains that abortion must be considered in the same way as other medical procedures, some nuances should be added.
From the strictly medical point of view, it is a medical procedure like others. But from a moral point of view, it is a very different kind of medical procedure. Indeed, as the Hon. Jake Epp said, "it is the only medical procedure that involves taking the life of an unborn child as a way to improve the quality of life for someone else, namely, the pregnant woman."
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-43 takes account of the Supreme Court judgement that, in ruling section 251 invalid, wanted the procedure to be less cumbersome.
Instead of three physicians, there will be only one. This reduction would be acceptable if the decision were made "after objective analysis of all other possible solutions", as the CMA's brief to the legislative committee says. But we must ensure that this analysis has been done properly. At one in his trials, Dr. Morgentaler admitted that he did nothing of the kind. In short, he performed abortion on demand, which is unacceptable; no surgical operation is performed on demand.
If Parliament decided to have a sort of committee do this analysis, this committee would have to be very flexible. First of all, the ultimate goal of such a committee should be to have as many women as possible who want to interrupt their pregnancy carry it to term by helping them to make an enlightened and responsible
Government Orders
decision. Otherwise, the number of abortions will not go down and the fine statements in favour of respect for life will come to naught.
However, this committee would not have to grant approval: it would simply confirm that the analysis the CMA mentioned had been done.
The woman involved would then make her decision by herself, thus respecting the moral aspect of this medical procedure since the conscience regulates morality: "Those who act according to their conscience, even when misguided, as long as they show goodwill, also obey the laws of God since they follow the first and only true principle of listening to their conscience". This is Saint Thomas Aquinas's moral philosophy. An act in keeping with the person's conscience is subjectively good even if it is a crime in itself.
In a sphere where there is no unanimity, even among supporters of the Catholic moral code, we must compensate for the often denounced vagueness of reasons for abortion by putting more faith into the sense of morality of the people involved. While the Catholic religion does not allow abortions under any circumstances, it makes them possible by invoking the first precept of the Catholic ethic: "Obey your conscience".
As for the second constraint imposed by the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, no sanctions should be taken against the people involved, such as doctors and nurses, as long as they follow the procedure outlined in the legislation.
Bernard Haring wrote: "Almost everywhere abortions performed by a physician for vital or simply therapeutic purposes are left unpunished". In terms of morality, not allowing is one thing but not punishing is another.
Finally, the bill extends the notion of health to mental and psychological health.
A legislator tormented by his conscience could include the "particularly painful cases" Haring was talking about.
Julien Harvey seemed to reassure them when he wrote: "The mother's distress and not only her physical health can justify, in conscience and in law, an abortion as a lesser evil in the first quarter of pregnancy, a restriction that a long religious tradition in the West

May 22, 1990
Government Orders
allows us to contemplate". This can be found in the September issue of Relations, at page 196.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, an abortion law would not come into conflict with the principles of Catholic morality, the most rigid of moral doctrines, as long as it contained the four following provisions: making abortion a crime when it is performed by a person other than a physician and providing for appropriate penalties; outlining a way of doing the "objective analysis of all the alternatives" the CMA was referring to; making the pregnant woman responsible for her own decision; not imposing penalties when this procedure has been followed.
This, Mr. Speaker, is only a very small part of my reflections. We could talk about it for hours but I would like to close by saying I will give the government my total support when we vote on this bill which of course is not perfect but, under the circumstances, tries to conciliate the various positions.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on Motion No. 10 to Bill C-43, as proposed by my hon. colleague from Glengarry-Prescott-Russell. This amendment, if adopted, would allow abortions to be performed only if the mother's life was threatened by the continuation of the pregnancy.
Since Bill C-43 first came before this House, various groups have presented their views to the legislative committee on an act respecting abortions. Thousands of Canadians have written to their members of Parliament, and several members of this House have proposed amendments to the bill.
The conviction of the people in the riding of Hillsborough, who I represent, has not wavered. The majority of my constituents and I believe that human life begins at conception, and it must be protected by law at all stages. With such a conviction, I cannot support Bill C-43 unless it is amended. The life of the unborn child must be protected by law and I could only support a bill which provides such protection.
I did vote for Bill C-43 at second reading, but I supported it so that the bill would go to a legislative committee where amendments could be proposed that would fully protect the life of the unborn child.
Even as I voted for it at second reading, I knew that the only exception to the full protection of the foetus which I could ultimately support, would provide that an abortion could be performed to save the mother's life. That is what the motion I am discussing proposes to do. If it is not adopted, then I cannot possibly support the bill.
If Bill C-43 were to pass as is, an abortion would be legal when performed for health reasons, whether for mental, physical or psychological factors. This is a flimsy disguise for abortion on demand, and Canadians will not condone such hypocrisy. Pro-abortion advocates would have us believe that if we deny women access to abortion on demand, we are denying them basic health care. I have several problems with that argument, but the most fundamental one is that we are dealing with two human lives here, not one.
I am horrified that anyone could say that a procedure which kills one human being for the convenience of another is a medical procedure. Abortion is the killing of a human being, and a helpless one at that. If we do not ensure that abortions are performed only to save the mother's life, then our society will be condoning abortion on demand.
We hear a great deal about freedom of choice. The rallying cry of the pro-abortion forces is that every woman must have the freedom to choose whether or not to bear children. I wholeheartedly agree that everyone must have the freedom to choose, but I say that the time for this choice is before conception takes place.
The choice to be made is whether to take the risk of conception occurring at all. Once a choice has been made and a human being has been created, the woman and her family have different choices to make. It is not true that after a pregnancy has begun there are no other options. The pro-abortion groups would have us believe it is a black and white situation, but that is not true.
Thousands of Canadian couples are infertile and long for a child of their own. Waiting lists at adoption agencies are years long. The so-called black market in babies exists, and the emergence of surrogate motherhood is evidence of the desperate longing of infertile couples to have children.
There are loving, stable homes for babies born to women whose families cannot support them. In view of
May 22, 1990

this, abortion on demand is an act of pure selfishness. I am not pretending that unwanted pregnancies are trivial or that they are easy experiences for people to live through. No one would deny that women with unwanted pregnancies, and their families, deserve all the support that we can give them during a very difficult time.
Support is the key, not denial. A healthy, humane, caring society must address the situation of unwanted pregnancies and not pretend that they do not happen. Abortion is a denial of the problem of unwanted pregnancy, and it is a denial of responsibility. Above all, it is a fundamental denial of the value of human life.
Bill C-43 completely fails to address the painful issue that is troubling this country's conscience. It fails to provide leadership on this fundamental, social and moral issue, which are the factors that drive women to seek abortions.
Abortion is not an answer to poverty, rape, sexual abuse, family violence or teenage pregnancy. It must not be allowed to become an escape from responsibility, either for the individual or for our society as a whole. I stated that I believe in the sanctity of human life, and that life begins at conception. Like all humans, unborn children deserve the full protection of the law. How can any civilized society which professes to care for the rights of the individual, which professes to be a world leader in human rights, deny these rights to one group simply because they are at a different stage of life. It is not a less valuable stage, not a less human stage, just a different stage, a totally vulnerable stage.
Our society has many problems to solve, such as the problem which led us to this dreadful situation in which thousands of abortions were performed every year. However, Bill C-43 as it stands is not an answer because abortion is not an answer. Bill C-43 must be amended to fully protect human life from conception onward. Only when the mother's life is threatened can abortion be considered an option, and with the advances in medical technology being made every day, I believe that this scenario has become an extremely rare one.
Mr. Speaker, if the motion of my colleague from Glengarry-Prescott-Russell is not adopted and if we do not change this bill so that the rights of the unborn
Government Orders
child are fully protected by law, then I must vote against this bill.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate most sincerely the opportunity to say a few words at report stage of Bill C-43, which as you are well aware, deals with the sensitive and very controversial issue of abortion.
My own views with respect to this matter of abortion are well known. I have spoken out in my own riding over the years, I have spoken out in other parts of Canada and I have spoken out in this House on numerous occasions, the last time being on November 23 of last year in the debate on second reading. In each case I made it quite clear where I stood, that I stand clearly and firmly on the pro-life side of the scale.
The bill before us at report stage has certain elements. As I pointed out in my remarks in this House on November 23 of last year, these elements support the pro-life position, in particular, the bill provides that abortion is an offence under the Criminal Code. It also rejects, and rejects quite clearly, the gestational approach to abortion and therefore it recognizes implicitly, if not explicitly, that life does begin at conception.
Having said that in my remarks at second reading, the bill as it now stands at report stage, is an extremely disappointing one for me. It is a bill which has many exemptions and a bill that is far wider than the sort of legislation that I would like to see before this House.
I had hoped that we would see some substantial amendments to this bill after it passed second reading and went to a legislative committee where the committee had an opportunity to examine it clause by clause to hear witnesses and to make amendments. I have been a member of numerous legislative committees in the past where very substantial amendments were made to legislation. Certainly I had hoped most fervently that we would see those kinds of amendments come from the legislative committee and that the bill at report stage would be an entirely different one from the one we see before us today.
Clearly, that did not happen and it has left me with a deep, extreme and profound sense of disappointment about what has happened to this bill. At the same time that presents me with a supreme dilemma, a dilemma of whether I am now in a position to support Bill C-43 in an unamended stage or not.

May 22, 1990
Government Orders
I do not like this bill. The Prime Minister has indicated that it is a free vote for other members of this House, but it is not a free vote for members of cabinet. That is a position that has left me deeply troubled. It has left me struggling with my conscience. It has left me with many sleepless nights. It has left me doing a great deal of praying as I am, quite frankly, right at this very moment.
I have come to the conclusion that this particular bill, no matter whether it passes this House or whether it does not pass this House, will not be the end of the great struggle for the pro-life side of the argument, for the pro-life movement on this issue. If this particular bill is defeated in this House, the pro-life struggle is going to continue. If this particular bill passes this House, the pro-life struggle is still going to continue.
Bearing in mind that no matter what happens to this particular legislation the struggle is going to go on, I have to face in my heart whether it is going to further the pro-life cause and further my own pro-life convictions to have one less voice in cabinet in support of the pro-life position and, in all likelihood, to have one more prochoice voice in cabinet contrary to the pro-life position.
As I say, I have struggled long and I have struggled hard and I still continue to struggle with this. I suspect that after the votes are cast, I will continue to search my soul and my heart on this particular issue.
However, I have come to the conclusion that, because this is not the end of the struggle and because the pro-life position is going to go on whether this bill passes or is defeated, rightly or wrongly, I am going to support this bill.
If I am wrong in that decision, then without a doubt it is the absolute duty of those who believe I am wrong to work their hardest and do their utmost to ensure my defeat at the next election.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on the amendments to Bill C-43, and in particular to support Motion No. 24.
I do this because I believe that a compassionate society and a Parliament elected to represent society's needs and society's wishes does not need to return to a time when women were criminals for exercising the most fundamental of human rights, that right being the
personal care and control of one's body. Reproductive choice is a basic and fundamental right.
I rise also to argue that the role of Parliament is not to imprison women forced to make difficult decisions, but rather to provide the leadership, the process and the money for better prevention of unplanned pregnancies, and to ensure that every child bom in this nation and every woman who chooses to be a mother has the opportunity to live a full and rich life, a life free of poverty, ignorance, violence and abuse.
We are not the first, nor will we be the last society to debate abortion. This has been an issue of conflict throughout history. If there is one thing that we have learned from history, it is that no matter what the law, or how tough the sanctions, abortion will happen. Abortions, if they are not performed legally in medical facilities under the direction of a physician, will happen in much less favourable circumstances. As ugly as it may seem, women must not be forced to return to those ugly circumstances of using coat hangers, vacuum cleaners, or putting themselves in the hands of quacks. It is an ugly reality, but it is a reality. Women die as a result of these kinds of processes. Young women are sterilized as a result of these kinds of procedures. The reality is that any amendment that puts abortion back in the Criminal Code will sentence some women somewhere in Canada to sterility or to death. That is not supporting life.
The bill before us and the amendments being debated today in many ways define the fundamental value and inherent dignity of each human being and the worth of each human life.

This debate cannot be used to convince people. That is impossible, and if we, as legislators, keep trying to do so, we would be losing our time and we would not be serving our constituents. What we ought to do is define the common goals we should strive to attain, which are to glorify life, to respect life and to reduce the number of abortions.
On one side, there are those who believe that to legislate criminal sanctions is the only way to reach our goals. On the other, there are those, like myself, who believe that the only way to reach our end is to develop social and economic policies which would ensure that every child, every woman, and even every family is respected and even glorified.
May 22, 1990

Government Orders

We have made this realization in other areas. It was not that long ago that attempting suicide was a criminal offence which appeared in the Criminal Code. Statistically, suicide attempts are most prevalent among young men and teenage boys. So do we threaten today to fill the prisons with young men attempting suicide? Do we believe that criminal sanctions will actually reduce the number of attempts? Of course not. We know that it is an emotional issue. It is an issue that needs to be dealt with in other ways.
We responded by removing attempted suicide from the Criminal Code and putting the emphasis where it belongs, on prevention and support. That was the right thing to do, just as ensuring that abortion remains decriminalized is the right thing to do.
There has been much said during this debate about respect for human life, about how our society and our nation is based on this respect. I say to the members of this Chamber and to Canadians everywhere, words are not enough. It is much easier for us to stand here and to legislate than to bend down and offer a helping hand to a child who has been abused, a woman who is tormented, or an unemployed father who is wondering how he is going to feed his family. The answer is clearly that this must be, and regardless of the law we pass here will continue to be, the choice of women.
I would like to draw this House's attention to what I think is a very good statement. This statement was made on July 27,1988, in this House by the present Minister of Employment and Immigration who stated:
And make no mistake, women make the right choice, a far better
choice than you or I or all the pageantry of institutions that have
been invented by human beings from the beginning of time.
I agree with that statement made by the Minister of Employment and Immigration. I believe she was reflecting that women are adults, that women can make the right choices, and whatever any institution decides to do, we will not be able to control the decisions of women. It must be the choice of all women. We know that women of wealth and power have options, and part of what we are debating today is whether or not that freedom will be extended to all women.
All women, not just the wealthy, must be free to decide the number and the spacing of their children. All children have the right to be raised in a family capable of providing housing and food and proper nurturing. All children have the right to be raised in a family free of violence and abuse.
If anyone believes that they can lay claim to a respect for life because they legislated against abortion, while voting for cuts to child care, cuts to shelters for abused women, cuts to job creation, cuts to prenatal health and prevention, then they are fooling themselves. They are not fooling the electorate, they are fooling themselves.
I am not going to debate which side of the question has a monopoly on the respect for life. I am pro-choice and I will put my commitment and my record of action up against anyone's when it comes to a respect for human life.

If we go beyond the legal, medical, and philosophical questions raised by this debate, we see that the real issue is, in fact, very simple. Who is to decide whether a pregnancy shoud be interrupted? Judges and lawyers? The Church? Or maybe politicians and legislators? Or should not the women, given their unique capability to conceive, look deep into their hearts and souls and make that decision?
I think those decisions should be the responsibilities of the women. They have heard every argument. They know that some families are eager to adopt children.
