I am warning all my colleagues for whom I have great esteem and who I wish will return to this House of Commons after the next election. Will the people support a member who supports a bill that is far more liberal than the bill we inherited from the Liberals when we took office in 1979?
If there is one amendment that I think has even the slightest chance of passing, I would vote for it and it alone and I would urge those who are really and truly pro-life to consider the same move. I would vote for Motion No. 10. Motion No. 10 would not satisfy Mother Teresa or Pope John Paul, but it would satisfy the majority of Canadian people if we were to support Motion No. 10.
However, the government has said today that it is not recommending any amendments, even the most minute amendment affecting very little of the functional ability of people to have abortions. The government is not interested in taking a serious look at any amendments.
So at report stage I would support one motion, Motion No. 10. At third reading I suspect we will not have Motion No. 10, or any other motion. For that reason at third reading I will vote the same way as I have voted for 12 years on this issue. I will take a pro-life stance. I will stand and defend it regardless of how many of my constituents tell me they will never vote for me again because I am pro-life. They told me that on capital
punishment, on metric and on extradition. If everybody who said they would not vote for me again ever got together in my riding I would not get any votes, I would be in a negative position.
The truth of the matter is that constitutents today look for members of Parliament who will come to Ottawa and try to do what they say they want to see done. In Canada today we have a strange collection of members of Parliament who are faced with conscience issues, party positions, government positions and constituency positions. Remember, members of Parliament will never go down in flames if they are consistent.
I am proud to say that I am voting against this bill and any other bill like it as long as I am fortunate enough to be here in this House of Commons.

Mr. Speaker, I had planned what I was going to say about the motions before I came into the House today, but when I listened to the motions that were presented, many things went through my mind. I felt some very strange emotions.
I had not felt these things when I had looked at the written words of the motions. One of the things that went through my mind was that each and every one of these anti-choice, more restrictive motions was being proposed by men in this House of Commons and that the only pro-choice motion was being proposed by a woman, and that was me.
I am the only mover of an amendment who has actually been pregnant, who knows what women go through when they are pregnant, who knows what they go through when they give birth to children, who knows what women go through when they contemplate the choices that are ahead of them when they find out they are pregnant.
I have three grown children. The complete ignorance and lack of real feeling of what women go through when they are pregnant, when they contemplate an abortion, when they contemplate adoption, or when they contemplate the future and keeping that child, was so evident by the statements made by the other movers of motions in this House today.
I was shocked to hear phrases such as "abortions are performed for cosmetic reasons, for frivolous reasons", and "abortion is an easy option for women". Someone said that women say to themselves that they just do not
May 22, 1990

like this pregnancy so they terminate it. That is nonsense and is insulting to the women of Canada.
One mover made a bizarre analogy between the criminal penalties for abortion and the penalties for negligence when you are towing a water skier behind you on a boat. Pregnancy is a unique experience; it is not like water skiing, it is not like driving a boat, it is not like arson, it is not like anything else. It is a joyous and wondrous experience for those who have chosen to become mothers, but it can be a very painful and disastrous experience for those whose pregnancy is unwanted.
One mover of an anti-choice motion spoke of how his personal experience of raising a disabled child had shaped his opinion on the whole issue of abortion. My first child was born with a genetic mutation. It is a very serious and life-threatening mutation. He is handicapped and he is disfigured from the medical treatment that he had to undergo. This experience did not make me want to suppress women's choices. It did not make me want to decide for other women what their choices should be. It did not make me want to take away another woman's right to decide the number or the spacing of her children. I made personal decisions to carry out my pregnancies. My personal experiences do not entitle me to decide for other women what their choices should be.
The member spoke of how glad he was that his adopted child had been available for adoption. Well, I wonder about the women and the young girls who are pressured and sometimes even forced to give up their newborn infants for adoption. They might keep those children if they had the financial means. The answer to this situation is to support pregnant women and families, not to expect poor women to give away their children to better-off or well-off people.
Neither abortion, adoption nor keeping a child is an easy decision. The only people who can say that these are easy decisions are those who will never, ever have to face that kind of a decision. Women around the world have risked their lives, their health, their fertility, to obtain abortions in countries where they are illegal, where there is no access to abortions. Women die because they will always make that choice for themselves. They will
Government Orders
not allow the state to dictate to them their own personal choices on this issue.
Making abortion illegal does not stop abortion. It simply makes it dangerous, unsafe and a potential killer of women.
Some of these motions, if passed, would amount to a death sentence for some Canadian women. One of these motions would have us throw our medical practitioners in jail for up to 20 years. Under the aiding and abetting section of the Criminal Code, women who have abortions would also be liable to a severe term of imprisonment.
This is the solution that some members of this House say is the answer to this very, very complex social issue; an answer that would put teenage girls into jail; one that would have the effect of jailing mothers who already may have young children, simply because they could not bring themselves to bear another child.
The mover of Motion No. 5 said in his statement, "when I think an abortion should be available". Well, Mr. Speaker, how arrogant, how patronizing to the women of Canada. How dare any member of this House set him or herself up as the sole judge of how many children other people should have, when they should have them and why they should have them. This is an abuse of our role as legislators. Our job is not to intrude into the private affairs of individuals and to make personal, very intimate and very painful decisions for them. The decision to have children or not is one of the most private, intimate and individual decisions there can be.
I am glad to see that the Liberal member who submitted a motion that would have made some forms of birth control illegal has withdrawn it. It would be fitting if some other movers of motions contemplated what their motions would really do to women's lives and health and withdraw theirs as well. It is so obvious that these movers of motions have never experienced an unwanted pregnancy and cannot even contemplate with any degree of realism what it means to be faced with these decisions.
Another thing that I noticed was that the movers all supported one another. There was great camaraderie among them. They congratulated each other for their motions. Well it is time that the women in this House of Commons supported one another.

May 22, 1990
Government Orders
I have received support from my caucus but I look forward to receiving what all the women in Canada need, the support of all members of this Elouse who value the fundamental right of every person to control their own bodies and their own lives, the right to decide whether or not they will have children and when.
Most Canadians believe in family planning education and in support for pregnant women and families. This is the real solution. A November Environics poll found that 62 per cent of Canadians are opposed to this government's plan to recriminalize abortion.
This bill is no compromise, Mr. Speaker, it is a sell-out. These amendments before us seek to make a bad bill, a criminal bill, even worse.
I heard one of the Tories who moved an amendment talk about social policy in addition to a criminal law. Well, the most effective approach is social policy instead of a criminal law. It is ironic that while he spoke of social policy, the government which he supports is busy dismantling Canada's social support network, making it economically more difficult for people to raise their children. Ele is part of a government that scrapped the national child care program, deindexed family allowances and put a cap on the Canada Assistance Plan, which is the federal-provincial funding mechanism that currently provides child care spaces and shelters for battered and abused women.
I listened to the member for Peterborough who spoke before me. Ele indicates that he would even change the Charter of Rights and Freedoms in this country. He would change it to stop women having their full rights. It is shocking. I am horrified to hear some of the comments that have been made here.
I would like to address some of the comments that the Minister of Justice made when she spoke to the amendments. The minister said three times that society has an interest in protecting the foetus. Why is this government criminalizing abortion which provides no protection for the foetus? Many groups and individuals have told us that. That was the overwhelming input from Canadians who came to the legislative committee hearings.
If the government really wants to protect the foetus, why is it not concerned about reproductive health
hazards in the workplace, the higher incidence of women and men becoming infertile in our community? Why is it not working toward those issues and toward the underlying issue that always exists when women choose abortion, that is, poverty?
I urge all members to vote against the amendments and to vote for Motion No. 24 which is the pro-choice amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to address the proposed amendments at report stage of Bill C-43. This is an issue that has touched every Canadian. It is an issue that I do not think anyone could have been elected to this House without addressing time and again in the various forums that led up to our election.
It is very obvious from the tone and tenor of the debate this afternoon on the amendments that everyone in the House recognizes how important this is. The debate is also being conducted in a manner in which I would like to see more of them conducted, with each member free to express his or her own point of view and to vote according to his or her own conscience or according to the wishes of his or her constituents.
Having said that, I do not know if very many of us are ready to handle the emotional weight that would be involved if we had to face many issues like this one.
The legislative committee that reviewed the bill deserves to be recognized and applauded for its work. It invested a tremendous amount of study and many hours in listening to witnesses and examining the same. It spent a lot of time in debate and in research. The members of the committee gave the issue much thought and did much soul-searching.
We all know that the bill was reported unamended. That does not mean that there was agreement, as we know. Far from it. This illustrates the problem that exists in trying to legislate a moral issue upon which there are greatly diverging views.
In my speech at second reading I said:
To achieve political solutions to the complex and controversial problems that come before us it is often necessary to accept compromise. On this issue, however, views are held so strongly and opinions are so galvanized that many of the people we represent are, because of personal convictions, unwilling or unable to compromise their position or their beliefs.
May 22, 1990

I went on to say:
Bill C-43 is by necessity a political answer to a moral question, and
as a political answer represents a compromise and moral values are
not subject to compromise.
My personal position is that life is sacred from the moment of conception until natural death. Many people who share that conviction with me have said that that they felt I compromised my views by supporting Bill C-43 at second reading. They asked how it was possible for me to accept a bill that was a compromise.
Politicians must face a reality that advocates outside of the legislative process do not have to face. We must sometimes accept a bill that is less than perfect when it is better than the alternative. At second reading the alternative was this bill or nothing. I supported it because it was better than the vacuum which existed, and which still exists. I supported it because it is still possible to strengthen it and provide more protection for the life of the unborn.
You cannot compromise moral values as an individual. It is not possible to compromise in your personal life and still retain those values. You are either right or you are wrong.
In the political process our values should be equally strong, but the reality is that to achieve political approval you need the support of half of the members of this House, and at this stage of the debate it is already becoming very apparent that it is going to be difficult to get that many members to support either extreme of the debate. We might well face the same question: not what is right or wrong; not what is the ideal; not what we would like; but what is best given the alternatives available.
The difficulty that the committee experienced illustrates just how difficult it is to achieve compromise in this moral issue, where strongly held opinions do not allow for it.
We are now engaged in debates on amendments at report stage, amendments that have the potential to either strengthen or weaken the bill and the protection it provides for the unborn.
In a brief presented to the legislative committee by the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops they said:
Government Orders
You have the responsibility of drafting legislation which will profoundly affect future generations. Your recommendations will be a statement about the value Canadians place on human life. Yours is not an easy task, but we are confident that you have the ability, humanity and integrity to make a difference.
Time does not allow us to present detailed responses to each of the many amendments and motions before us today. These amendments could make a tremendous difference to the bill. It is my intention to support those amendments which offer more protection for the life of the unborn.
Bill C-43, as presented and reported, still makes an important statement about the importance of life. It recognizes that importance from the moment of conception. It states that it is a criminal act to abort that life unless the health or life of the mother, who carries that life, is threatened.
The weakness, from my perspective, is that the definition of "health" is too broad and not restrictive enough. No one at committee, or in debate, ever argued that abortion should be a form of birth control and we do not want it to be. I will be supporting those amendments that restrict abortion to those circumstances where, in the opinion of a medical practitioner, the life of the mother is threatened.
The committee, in preparing its report, heard numerous witnesses and much testimony. As did many other members of the House, I accepted the opportunity to sit in and participate in the committee when the opportunity allowed. It was an emotional and draining experience. Those who sat throughout all of the hearings have my admiration.
During one of my visits to the committee, a presentation was made by a group called Women for Social Justice. This group will not agree with my position in its entirety, but I would like to quote two statements from their brief to the legislative committee. They said, first: "It is a strength of Bill C-43 that it acknowledges that all society has an interest in unborn persons".
It is not enough in this issue just to talk of women's rights. We cannot perpetuate the myth that men have no responsibility. Indeed we have legislated rights, but all too often we have ignored the requirement that we have to accept responsibility for our actions. If this country is going to continue to reflect the values it was built on, we

May 22, 1990
Government Orders
must understand and accept the fact that responsibility must precede rights.
One of the values our society has always respected is the value of life and I pray that we will strengthen our law to the extent of respecting the value of the life of the unborn as well.
In their presentation to the legislative committee, Women for Social Justice also said: "It is the function of the criminal law to symbolize our social ideals. Abortion is an issue about the most basic social value and therefore belongs in the central document of our law, codifying community commitment".
Another group representing Catholic Bishops stated, referring to the committee, but it would apply equally well to the House today as we consider these amendments, that our recommendations will be a statement about the values that Canadians place on human life.
Reflecting on this, I would suggest that no stronger statement could be made about the value that Canadians place on life and on the importance of the rights of the individual than guaranteeing the rights of those who are most vulnerable and protecting their right to life. Even with the proposed amendments we do not guarantee the right to life for the unborn, but we can make a strong statement about the value Canadians place on life and establish legal recognition of unborn persons. I would encourage all hon. members of this House to respect life and support those amendments that provide more protection for the unborn.

Mr. Speaker, I want to remind members, first, of what I said in this House when I spoke against Bill C-43 last November. I said that to those of us who are older, life itself takes on a new meaning. I, as a farmer, go out in the spring of the year to the fields and pastures and see life all about us. We see the birds, the animals, the new growth, the trees, the grass and the flowers, and there is a sense of nearness to one's Creator, the Creator of human life, of life itself.
This debate is about human life, the lives of unborn children. I ask the members of this House to consider the lives of these unborn children above all else.
You will note that the Scriptures never talk about the foetus, they always talk about the child in the mother's womb. An example is Isaiah 49.15: "Can a woman forget
the infant at her breast, or a mother the child of her
womb?"
I want to draw to the attention of this House that in the preamble to our Constitution it is stated that Canada was founded on principles recognizing the supremacy of God and the rule of the law. I accept those principles, but I further believe in the sanctity of human life and I will work and fight to protect the rights of the unborn. Bill C-43 does not offer any protection to those rights.
I commend my colleague from Glengarry-Prescott- Russell who brought in Motion No. 10. Motion No. 10 would delete the word "health" as a reason for abortion. This would mark a substantial change in the nature of Bill C-43. If amended by Motion No. 10, the passage of Bill C-43 would be a clear indication that Parliament does not want the lives of unborn children placed at risk or to have those lives snuffed out.
The passage of Motion No. 10 would be a step in the right direction. Without the passage of Motion No. 10, Bill C-43 would simply remain a formula for abortion on demand. We would regard a vote for Bill C-43 in these circumstances, regardless of any other amendments passed, as unacceptable.
I certainly commend my colleague from Glengarry- Prescott-Russell on his amendment to this bill and for his endeavours to give some protection to the lives of unborn children.
It is interesting to note that Nurses for Life recognize abortion as the taking of an innocent human life and advocate legislation to protect the youngest members of the human family. It is interesting that this group of nurses and many doctors feel very strongly about this issue.
I want to quote from a letter from a family practitioner in my riding. He says:
I feel very strongly that this Bill C-43 is merely a method of fully legalising abortion on demand. In saying "-a medical practitioner who is of the opinion that-the health-of a female person would be likely to be threatened" and then that "-health includes- psychological health - " the act opens the way to any physician to perform any abortion on the pretext that continuing the pregnancy would endanger her psychologically.
In Britain, about 20 years ago, a very similar bill was introduced with the additional factors of requiring two doctors and a gestational limit. This law immediately resulted in abortion on demand with no practical redress.
May 22, 1990

This approach totally ignores the right of the unborn human being to life. This is a God-given right which the state cannot morally take away.
As a physician of 25 years' qualification I should like to mention that I have never seen or heard of a case in which the mother's life was lost by continuing her pregnancy when in the natural place of within the uterus. Occasionally we do see ectopic or tubal pregnancies which are not in the natural site but usually these are only diagnosed after the baby has already been lost.
As I mentioned earlier, as we look at the events unfolding around us in the world today at this time of year, a season when we have the creation of life all around us, it is very ironic that we as the Parliament of Canada are debating a bill that would end life, particularly human life.
I want to quote from another letter. It says:
Before Bill C-43 has its third reading, I would like to express my concerns regarding this bill. Bill C-43 has been characterized as a compromise between the pro-abortion position and the pro-life position. In actual fact, however, it virtually opens a door to abortion on demand. For it is a known fact, that abortions can easily be obtained when they are allowed for so-called health reasons. Even the restrictions "physical, mental and psychological" will not prevent this, for they are too general and too vague.
It goes on to say:
I urge you to withdraw this bill and to give our country an abortion law that protects all of Canada's children from the moment of conception. Only when you do that can we expect God to look down upon our country in favour and grant us His blessing.
It is signed by Reverend Dick Moes of Strathroy, Ontario.
I have another letter that I want to read. It is from an RNA from Kitchener, Ontario. She says:
I am writing to you as an adoptee. When I was 3 months old, I was officially adopted, and have had 19 wonderful years with my adoptive parents. One thing really bothers me: when I was still in the womb, my biological mother could have aborted me, and although it was 1969, abortions were still available.
I think of how my life could have been ended in a few short minutes, before I'd seen my first sight. How then can we actually stand back and allow leniency in the laws for abortion, when millions of unborn children will never see the light of day.
I implore you to see how fragile and precious life is, and how innocent the foetus is, no matter what circumstances their conception comes from. Please -life is so important-say no to abortion. Sincerely,
Government Orders
How can we ignore this, particularly at this time of year when we have a bill like this one before us. Certainly my colleague from Glengarry-Prescott-Russell realized the implications or he would never have brought forward an amendment such as Motion No. 10.1 believe it has to be included or we have to turn down this bill as practically no law at all or it would allow abortion on demand.
We have to look at the conscience of this nation and look to the preamble of our Constitution, when it was pointed out so very clearly that Canada was proud of those principles recognizing the supremacy of God and the rule of the land. My plea here today is to ask members of Parliament to make sure that those two principles are not in conflict: one is God's teaching which reflected the supremacy of God and the other is the rule of the land and the decision of this Parliament with regard to this bill that hits so close to the hearts of all of us here today.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for the opportunity to speak on this motion and to say again that I am opposed to this bill unless it is amended with Motion No. 10 which my colleague has put forward in this House.

Mr. Speaker, I rise again to speak further on this subject.
I put forth Motion No. 17B which dealt with the definition of health and read:
"physical and menial health, and does not include psychological".
My amendment was part of two others put forth by the member for Kitchener and the hon. member for Fraser Valley East. They were both as well pro-life amendments. I also support, as I said earlier in the day, Motion No. 10 put forth by the hon. member from Glengarry- Prescott-Russell.
In speaking on the amendments I want to make the point and share some thoughts on why I believe Bill C-43, even if it is not amended, is better than no legislation at all. If Bill C-43 is defeated, it will be years or decades before any government will have the political will to take the initiative and present proposed legislation to the House.
With the expected rapid developments in reproductive technologies, we may never again debate an abortion bill in this House. Amendments may be proposed and passed

May 22, 1990
Government Orders
to existing legislation, but we cannot make amendments if no bill exists. If some of us like myself are not happy with Bill C-43, we could look forward in the future to some amendments.
Several pro-life supporters have told me that I would be breaking my word if I voted for Bill C-43.1 want to say that those comments have disturbed and distressed me, but I have given the issue a great deal of thought. I have had many discussions and written correspondence with constituents. I have discussed the issue extensively in Ottawa with my pro-life colleagues and I have prayed about the issue. I believe for a number of reasons that it is better to have Bill C-43 than nothing at all.
I would like to quote from a book prepared by the Law Reform Commission entitled Rights of the Foetus in which it answers the question: Why the criminal law? It reads: "Through our criminal law we express the kind of society we believe in and the values we uphold. In our working paper 58 Commissioner Maingot, in his dissent, summarizes what criminal law means to us. The criminal law is our nation's fundamental statement of public policy- Ultimately, the criminal law is a mirror of what we are; it reflects our commitment, or lack of commitment, to human dignity and equality".
The book continues: "By using the criminal law power as the basis for a new law on abortion, we are enshrining a certain set of values, which in part describes the kind of society we are".
A second quote I would like to read into the record concerns another paragraph by the Law Reform Commission. It deals with the role of the Criminal Code in our society. It reads: "In truth, the criminal law is fundamentally a moral system. It may be crude, it may have faults, it may be rough and ready, but basically it is a system of applied morality and justice. It serves to underline those values necessary or else important to society. When acts occur that seriously transgress essential values like the sanctity of life, society must speak out and reaffirm those values. This is the true role of criminal law".
It should also be remembered that if we leave a legislative void some provinces will feel obliged to pass an abortion bill. In theory, we could have a patchwork quilt of provincial abortion laws. I find this possibility
unacceptable. Whatever abortion legislation we have should be uniform across the country.
In conclusion, as a pro-lifer we have at least three prime conditions. First, we must have a law on this area and it must be in the Criminal Code. Second, there must be provision for criminal sanction against an unlawful abortion, and that is in Bill C-43. Third, we must have protection of new life from conception or implantation. While not totally acceptable, these three conditions are in Bill C-43, but it should be noted that no gestation period is mentioned. I urge all hon. members to support Motions Nos. 10, 12, 13, and 17B.

Mr. Speaker, I am privileged to have the opportunity to place some of my thoughts on the record with respect to Bill C-43.
At the outset I want to say that I find the issue of abortion troublesome, complex, and intensely personal. I am very thankful to be in a position to cast a vote against Bill C-43 according to my conscience. I cannot afford the women of Canada anything less than to allow them to decide the issue according to their consciences.
I note that there are members opposite who normally support this government who have chosen to follow their consciences and vote against this government bill. They are doing so because they feel it is the right thing to do according to their consciences. For some reason they will not extend that same privilege or right to the women of Canada. I find that very difficult to understand.
What is this debate all about? I think it is really about who should decide the issue of abortion. It has nothing to do with one side having more respect for life than the other side. One side of this issue calls itself pro-life, while the other side calls itself pro-choice. In my long years of professional life I worked with hundreds of pro-choice women. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that they have just as much respect for life as those who call themselves pro-life.
It certainly has nothing to do with abortion on demand, a term that I find insulting, to tell the truth. I think it is an affront to women. I know of no woman who would equate the seeking or the contemplation of abortion with just another item on a shopping list. Yet, when people use that term, in effect they are saying that women
May 22, 1990

would look upon seeking an abortion just like buying something at the store.
Who should decide the issue of abortion? When all the rhetoric and arguments are cut away, who is going to decide? Is it the woman or the state? I can say truthfully and with all candour that I come down on the side of the woman.
Abortion is intensely intimate, intensely personal, and intensely complex. I cannot think of anyone in a better position to decide the delicate, troublesome issue than the woman. She is in the best position.
How can we come down on the side of an intrusive state? Where is the state in this matter? If we give the state the right to decide on the issue of abortion, it would have to do it from the position of one act or one law. It would have to make the profound decision at a distance, remotely. I cannot believe for a moment that even if we consider the odds the state could anywhere match the judgment of a woman who has to live with this matter from the moment of conception. I will choose the woman in this matter.
A woman is not perfect. She is a human being like the rest of us. She is not perfect. If you cannot trust a woman, who can you trust? Women are our mothers. If we cannot trust women about something as sacred as life, when it comes to unborn babies, when it comes to foetuses, who can we trust? I cannot believe that there are those who would trust the state before trusting the women of this world.
It is normal for women to have babies. It is normal for women to want to carry their pregnancies to full term. When a woman contemplates abortion she is sending out a very disturbing signal. She is saying that despite the fact God has given her the capacity to bring life into the world, she feels she cannot cope. There is something there that prevents her from bringing life into the world. I have to respect that judgement. I have to honour women.
Let us not forget that this issue really is a part of history, part of a continuum. There was a time when we did not trust women with the vote. We did not trust women to work outside the home. We did not trust women to enter professional classes. We thought they were best at home looking after the children or playing the part of housewife and housekeeper. We did not want them in managerial positions. In fact, there are still not
Government Orders
many women in managerial positions today. We certainly did not want women to control the purse strings in the home.
Women have been partly emancipated over the past number of years and what have been the results? Is the world poorer? Is our society poorer because women have gone out to enter professional ranks, managerial ranks and achieve equality with men in some areas? I do not think so.
I am opposed to this bill because it does not contribute in any way to the emancipation of women. Women have come a long way but they still have a great distance to go.
I had a mother who belonged to a generation of women who were very repressed. My mother was good enough to bring 14 children into the world. She helped raise 12. I suspect she pretty well raised them on her own. I was number 11. She was good enough to work around the clock, day and night, to raise these children. She was good and noble enough to serve as a wife. She was good and noble enough to serve as an unpaid servant of the family. She was perhaps the finest woman I ever knew and probably will ever know. What did she get in return? She got love from all of us. But, she could not participate in the major decisions of the family.
We were raised on a farm. Despite all the noble deeds, did she have a right to participate in the major decisions of running the farm? Not on your life. Did she have the right to participate in major spending decisions? Not on your life. While she would never have contemplated it, if she had ever thought for a moment about abortion or divorce or anything like that, her thoughts would not have been considered for a moment, because when it came to issues like that she was a second class citizen. I remember in those days how powerless my mother was and it was mainly because she was a woman. She was not entitled to participate in those major decisions.
I have heard a number of members today talk about the need to protect the foetus. I do not think anyone would disagree with that, whether they call themselves pro-choice, pro-life, or anything in between. We all want to protect the foetus, we all want to protect the unborn, we all want to protect life, we all want to respect life. I suggest that the best way to protect the unborn is to protect their mothers. One does not protect the foetus

May 22, 1990
Government Orders
through the Criminal Code, through some coercive law. We protect them by protecting their mothers.
That is another reason why I am against C-43. It does nothing in the way of providing community support. There is nothing in it dealing with child care. There is nothing to indicate that society will help women; that the community will help a woman to have her baby by providing the assistance she needs.
If we as a society want to protect the unborn, as we should, then let us protect the women and let us protect the mothers of the unborn.
I simply want to say in conclusion that a decision about abortion is complex and personal and intimate. We must leave it to the women. We have to learn to respect women and to trust their judgment. If we do that we will do more to protect life and the unborn than the state ever could.

Mr. Speaker, as Parliamentarians we have a responsibility to shape and enact a law that will respect human life from conception to natural death. I oppose abortion, the killing of the unborn. The so-called progressive-minded people who promote the concept of free abortion on demand are contravening the laws of nature and God.
I rise to support Motion No. 10 submitted by the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell. With the removal of the word "health" the clause would read: "If the abortion were not induced the life of the female person would be likely to be threatened."
The inclusion of the word "health" in Bill C-43 opens the door to many abuses, as happened with the former abortion bill in 1969. Its interpretation is open to many flimsy excuses as a justification for termination. When the word "health" is present, there is a need to define what it means. The plain fact is that it is extremely rare for a pregnant woman's health to be seriously in jeopardy as a result of pregnancy.
There may be other factors causing a health problem. In those instances the medical profession is already aware that they have a responsibility to treat that health problem without making a direct intervention on the life of the child. In the 1969 legislation all kinds of interpretations of health came into play, resulting in abortions being performed for reasons that were not always valid.
In the last 20 years, the large majority of abortions performed in Canada have been for reasons of convenience only, having nothing to do with the real meaning of health. I refer to the Badgley report on the operation of the abortion bill. It states: "In the majority of cases, stating that pregnancy is a danger to the patient's physical health is nonsense as there is no real threat to the patient's health if the pregnancy goes on."
Let us stop playing games with words by hiding the true reason for the slaughter. It is not for reasons of health, but rather for convenience. We must speak out for the sanctity of life.
speakername: Mr. Walter Van  De Walle@St. Albert

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak to the amendments put forward on this bill.
Before I address specific amendments, I would like to outline again for the House my own philosophical position on the issue. I think it is very clear that the decision a woman makes about an abortion is very personal and intense. It is a difficult issue. It is not done frivolously as some people in this House have suggested, and it is not done without due consideration. It is an agonizing decision.
The decision to have an abortion is a private issue that should not be subject to public or legal scrutiny and certainly should not be subject to legal sanction of the woman or her doctor. I have some understanding for those who oppose abortion under any circumstances because of moral conviction, but I cannot agree with them. They are at least consistent in their belief that under no circumstances should there be an abortion.
This bill is based on a fundamental concept that we, in this House, are able to make a decision on when a woman should have an abortion and that we are in a better position to make a more rational, moral and correct decision than that woman. I cannot agree with that. The women of Canada are totally competent to make the decision as to when they should have an abortion.
We do not know all the circumstances that they are going to be facing. We do not know the circumstances of their health or economics, and we do not know the circumstances or the dynamics of their families. A woman must take all these things into consideration

May 22, 1990

when she makes that decision. We think we can sit here and prejudge the circumstances under which a woman will be allowed or denied access to a medical abortion, perhaps forcing her to seek an abortion elsewhere.
Perhaps we should consider how we arrived at the position in which we now find ourselves. In 1988, the Supreme Court struck down the previous legislation. In doing so, Justice Wilson stated that the right to reproduce or not to reproduce, which is the issue in this case, is one such right, and is properly perceived as an integral part of a modem woman's struggle to assert her dignity and worth as a human being.
This legislation is not about allowing a woman to assert her worth and dignity as a human being. Chief Justice Dickson stated that by interfering with bodily integrity, forcing a woman by threat of criminal sanction to carry a foetus to term unless she meets criteria unrelated to her own priorities and aspirations is a profound interference with a woman's body and thus, is an infringement on the security of persons.
My philosophy is that it is a woman's right, and that she is the person best able to make that decision. Canadian women have the strength, intelligence, integrity, and, most of all, the right to decide when and under what circumstances they will bear children.
One of the reasons I think people oppose the position of pro-choice is that they think by putting in criminal sanctions it will deny women the right to have an abortion. That is not the history of Canada. It is not the history of any country that has had criminal legislation prohibiting abortion.
Prior to being elected, I worked in the social services field. I worked with poor women and street women. I worked with women who, because of various circumstances, found that they were not in a position either to wish or to be able to go through with a pregnancy. They were forced to seek abortions outside the law.
I have known women who have died from having abortions performed by unqualified practitioners. I can assure the House that, no matter what law is in place, women in urban centres, women with money, will always
Government Orders
get abortions. They will get them from medical practitioners. They always have.
It is the poor women who must to seek non-medical abortions. It is women in isolated and rural areas. It is women who do not understand the law, social agencies, and organizations who will be forced to seek illegal abortions. The sophisticated woman, the woman with money, the woman in the urban centre, is not going to be deterred by any piece of legislation that the House passes.
If the government really wanted to have an impact on abortions, then instead of trying to criminalize abortions again it should look to tiying to provide support for women. First, it should provide more support so that a woman has a choice as to whether or not she should become pregnant. She should have better information and better access to birth control.
Then, we must make it possible for the woman to make a choice in the true sense about whether she wishes to proceed with a pregnancy. We must provide her with child support, day care, and adequate wages. In this country, women are still paid only 66 per cent of the wages of men. We have to provide adequate housing so that she is able to say: "I am going to be in a position to raise this child in a secure environment".
But what has the government done? It has done everything it can to undermine the ability of women to make that choice. It has done away with the concept that it is going to bring in a universal child care program.
The government has made an absolute shambles of the housing program so that we now have an increasing number of Canadian families being forced into poverty because of inadequate housing. Housing is one of the main indicators of poverty in the country and we still have 1.2 million people living in poverty.
The government has put a cap on the Canada Assistance Plan, the social services network that can provide not only income support services to women but counselling services and such things as alternate home care for teenagers facing pregnancy. It has simply said that it is going to turn its back on the disadvantaged, the poor, and the person who is not socially and economically powerful. Then, at the same time, it wants to say: "We are also going to restrict your access to abortion".
I will close by saying that I will be opposing all of the amendments, except the amendment proposed by my

May 22, 1990
Government Orders
colleague from New Westminster. Hers is the only amendment that will protect the dignity and worth of women in the country.

Mr. Speaker, I want to intervene just briefly in this debate since I have already spoken my piece at second reading. I will not belabour the issue for long.
I do want to make it clear that I will be voting against this legislation. I will be voting against it because I believe in the sanctity of human life, and I mean all human life, from the moment of conception until natural death.
It strikes me as rather odd that we go through such extensive routines in the case of criminal activity to make sure that there is no miscarriage of justice. Yet we have before us a bill that says a life can be snuffed out by the decision of one person. I believe that is wrong. I believe that that is virtually abortion on demand. I believe that life is more sacred than that and that it deserves more protection.
Once we open the door to abortion, we are opening a Pandora's box that will be very difficult to close. We insist that every perpetrator of a crime-and I am repeating this because I think it is very important- every perpetrator of a crime has every access to the law. Yet, the government is bringing in a law that gives absolutely no protection to the human foetus, which is a fully human being except that it is not yet able to sustain itself. It has all the characteristics and all the attributes of a human being from the moment of conception. Therefore, in my opinion, it deserves full protection of the law from that very moment of conception until its natural death.
We have heard a lot of argument here about how onerous pregnancy is for the woman and, indeed, in some cases it is. But, in this day and age, there are the methods and access to methods of limiting the size of families. It would seem to me that we should be putting the emphasis and the education on that aspect of limiting family size, rather than expending all our time and efforts trying to find a way to kill the unborn child legally. I do not believe there is a way. I will not vote for this bill.

speakeroldname: Mr. Len Gustafson (Parliamentary Secretary to Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity to address our government's proposed abortion legislation. It is a bill of some significance because the principle on
which it is based reaches down and touches the very conscience of our nation. It makes a statement about the definition of life and lays out sanctions that symbolize our value of life.
During my years here, I have gone on record as one who believes that life begins at conception and at that miraculous point it acquires intrinsic worth and value. I am convinced therefore that from this point life should be protected and abortion allowed only when the life of the mother is threatened.
My position today remains unchanged. It is an extension of my desire to develop an anti-abortion consensus in our society.
I have no reason to believe that this consensus does not exist in the riding of Souris-Moose Mountain which I have the privilege to serve. Over the last months I have received 541 letters in favour of this position and two against.
This position is based on sound medical evidence. Those things which indicate life and determine who we are as individuals are present from conception. Clearly, we in this Chamber cannot ignore these facts. They are evidence which require a verdict in favour of truth and in favour of life.
Bill C-43 makes a statement about the truth of life. I am glad that it implicitly recognizes that life begins at conception by placing a criminal sanction against the taking of foetal life. In doing this, the law symbolizes our value and belief in the worth of life.
I might say at this point that I was pleased to see that the gestational approach is not in the bill, but that it does recognize the worth of life. The worth of life is not determined by its validity, its potential, whether it is wanted or not, or whether it will be productive to society or not. If these factors are allowed to determine the value of life before birth, how will we decide what protection life will be guaranteed after birth? We must acknowledge life as intimately valuable.
So, in giving the right to life to the unborn, we preserve life for all, honourable in what we give and what we preserve.
Having said that the bill is sound in principle, I am disappointed in its provision which lays out the conditions under which abortions would be permitted. The bill permits abortion not only for the legitimate reason of the
May 22, 1990

life of the mother, but for health reasons broadly defined as physical, mental and psychological.
I am deeply concerned that this definition of health is wide open to abuse. I am unhappy that it might allow abortions for reasons of convenience.
However, Bill C-43 does indicate that the mother and the doctor must make a moral choice. For this reason I have searched my heart long and hard. I have come to the conclusion that, because it is sound in principle, I will support this bill with reservations and with the vital hope and desire that it can be improved upon if not now, then at some time in the future.
As a Canadian parliamentarian I have two goals. It is my strongest desire as a parliamentarian to protect the value of life in law. But as a Canadian I have a strong desire to see a reorientation of our society to a view where abortions would be unthinkable. In fact, the two goals go hand in hand. Restricting abortions is easy when it is based on the wider consensus about the value of life.
I would go further to suggest to our pro-life friends that, while we in Parliament do our jobs, their efforts must be more directed to the building of a consensus. This can only be done through compassion and law. Our churches, organizations and we as individuals need to show a new direction that upholds concern over confrontation and that is marked by compelling compassion. We need to be part of the solution by building social, spiritual and physical support networks to serve the needs of the family and the single parent.
We cannot let it be said that our love ends after we succeed in entrenching pro-life legislation. If, while we fight for pro-life law, we lose sight of the greater compassionate purpose, then the law would be worthless.
Therefore I am pleased to say that I do support the protection of the foetus. While I am not completely supportive of the legislation, I believe that at this time it is the best that can be achieved under the circumstances that exist. I believe that a law is important.
I say to those who agree with me that one day we will achieve pro-life legislation. I do not believe for a minute that it is going to come with one stroke of a pen. As we are educated to the great miracle of life and the great
Government Orders
responsibility of protecting it, I believe one day we will have this legislation. I believe that the pro-life movement has to look forward in a positive way to directing its emphasis on how best this can be accomplished. It may be one step at a time, but that is my goal. I believe it should be the goal of all Canadians.
Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands-
Canso): Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this very important debate on an issue of fundamental importance, not only to the people of my riding but to all Canadians.
I want to begin by saying that I will be voting for the pro-life motions that were introduced earlier today. In particular, I will be supporting the motion which would restrict abortion to situations in which the life of the mother is threatened.
Second, I will be supporting the body of motions which would strengthen the health definition contained in the bill in order that that particular definition may limit, as far as possible, the circumstances in which abortion would be permitted.
I will be voting for those motions and expecting a number of them to carry in order to consider voting for the bill at third reading. In my view it is the only philosophically consistent approach I can take. It is the only approach which is consistent with a rigorous examination of what it is to be human, what it is to be Christian, what it is to believe in the sanctity of life and to support life in our laws, in our social customs and in our institutions.
However, I want to say at the outset that I would not like to have this be a blind pro-life versus a pro-choice distinction which is governing my decision in this matter. I believe that the dichotomy between these two points of view is far too simplistic an approach to understanding what is a very complex issue.
In fairness, I do not believe that those who proclaim themselves to be pro-choice are actually in favour of abortion. Likewise, I do not believe that those who proclaim themselves to be pro-life are against any form of choice, against the responsibility of women, against women, or against their particular freedom because they advocate restrictive legislative bounds on abortion.

May 22, 1990
Government Orders
I believe that the way to understand the principle of legislation to restrict abortion is in terms of social responsibility. We can regard laws as a curtailment or a restriction on human freedom, just like we could regard this particular law as a restriction on the choice or on the freedom of women, but I would rather see the law be regarded as a support for responsible social behaviour.
Seen in that light, it is no different than seeing, for example, seat-belt laws as legislation which restricts our freedom but, at the same time, encourages people to responsible social behaviour, just like other laws which, for instance, have imposed severe sanctions on consumption of alcohol while driving a motor vehicle. Those laws which have been introduced over the past few years, including social proscriptions, have also been an inducement to responsible social behaviour. And I think there is a way of understanding a restriction on abortion in that respect.
We must see, as a society, legislation which will encourage not only women, but men as well, to view the consequences of their actions, and particularly, in this case, into the sexual sphere, before they get into situation. The law has to support responsible conduct in this regard, realizing, of course, that situations in life will always make it difficult and will pose challenges for us as human beings when confronted with standards which would be established by, for example, a restrictive abortion law.
That having been said, I would like now to comment on some of the proposed motions of other hon. members, particularly those about which I feel most strongly.
Motion No. 16, which has been grouped for debate with my own, adds that a health risk must be a serious one. I agree. Requiring that the health risk be a serious one eliminates as a reason for abortion many of the quite normal physical and mental discomforts which often accompany a pregnancy.
I must stress again that any abortion law must be accompanied by a range of programs which address difficulties like the ones that have been mentioned by other speakers. Counselling services and medical advice must be available and accessible to all Canadian women. We must adopt a broad policy to effectively reduce abortions in Canada. A law by itself is insufficient and I
will speaking to that question at a later time, Mr. Speaker.
The last resort amendment, which is that abortions are only a last resort, must be accompanied by my own which narrows the health definition. What medically acceptable alternative treatment is there for psychological, socioeconomic factors such as being poor or being afraid to tell one's parents? Would treatment by a financial adviser or by a school counsellor constitute medically acceptable treatment to alleviate the health risk? This amendment is meaningless to me unless accompanied by a more restrictive definition of health.
Motion No. 13 interests me as well. It states that abortion be the treatment of last resort to alleviate the health risk to the mother.
The Canadian Medical Association has stated that abortion reflects a distasteful failure of the education and medical system. Abortion is a regrettable last resort treatment.
This last resort amendment must be accompanied by my own which limits the health definition to mental and physical. This amendment is meaningless to me unless a medically acceptable alternative treatment is found for psychological factors, such as being poor or afraid to tell one's parents.
Motion No. 19 expands the definition of opinion. The Canadian Medical Association has called Bill C-43's definition of "opinion" rather useless. Bill C-43 indicates that the medical communities practice acceptable standards deemed appropriate for formulating an opinion regarding abortion.
So why has the government bothered to insert it into the legislation? In my view, unless opinion is given additional and more defined meaning, insertion of its definition into Bill C-43 is useless.
In closing, Bill C-43 is in dire need of amendment. Motion No. 17A, which I have proposed, is only a minor change, but serves to clarify and strengthen the section of the bill which I feel is in need of repair. I cannot emphasize enough the urgent need of a broader policy on abortion in Canada, one which does not simply put a line into the Criminal Code but adds a program which will effectively reduce and hopefully eliminate the number of abortions in Canada.

May 22, 1990

Mr. Speaker, I am not pleased to be rising this evening to participate in this debate on the amendments to Bill C-43, an act regarding abortion.
I have listened with a growing sense of outrage to the statements by the men who are proposing, in total, 13 amendments. All of their amendments would make an already punitive bill even more so.
I try to insulate myself from that anger. I struggle to keep my temper in the face of these horrendous insults to women. I hope this evening to keep my temper sufficiently in order to speak clearly on this issue.
Earlier in today's debate the Minister of Justice told this House that the bill is a compromise, a fragile balance between a woman's right to control her own body and foetal rights. This is an outrageous statement coming from the woman given the honour of being the chief lawmaker in Canada.
Does the Minister of Justice not know that foetal rights have not been defined? The Supreme Court in the Daigle decision acknowledged that fact. The minister's statements this afternoon only served to exacerbate the confusion over this bill.
I will agree with the minister that Bill C-43 is a compromise, but the word compromise infers a solution. In this instance the so-called compromise is anything but a solution. It serves to mark a compromise of principle while moving us further from a solution.
If members of this Chamber were sincere in their wish for a real solution, they would be devoting much greater energy to the issues of equality for women, child poverty, reproductive health and education. They would be urging that greater resources be allocated for research into safe and effective means of birth control.
As a woman, I have had first-hand knowledge with that. When I was pregnant with my son, who is now 17 years old, I participated in a family planning clinic and took birthing classes. Of the 10 white, middle-class couples in that class, all well-educated people, six were there because of failed birth control. If this country really cared about stopping abortion, it would be putting more money into research into effective means of birth control.
Government Orders
I am ashamed of the ignorance that has been displayed in this Chamber on this issue. When I speak of ignorance I am giving those who speak the benefit of the doubt. If it is not ignorance, then it comes down to a conscious exercise of power, men utilizing their power over women. That is a very frightening and sinister prospect. Pregnancy is a wondrous process. It is wondrous for both women and men, but women are the only ones who can actually experience it. Some have argued that men are in awe, in fact resentful of that fact, that they have used their power to attempt to control the reproductive power of women. These men depict women as wanton creatures, morally deficient creatures, requiring threat of criminal sanction to keep them in line. It is this insulting assumption which is the basis of this law.
Some of the sanctimonious statements I have heard from men in the House today are trotted out as truisms, as items not considered by women facing an unwanted pregnancy. That is utter hogwash.
Absolutely.

Women facing an unwanted pregnancy do not need the advice of men in this House. I urge the members of this House, if they really truly respect women, to support the only amendment worthy of consideration, that is Motion No. 24 put forward by my honourable colleague-and I say that in the most sincere way-the hon. member for New Westminster-Burnaby.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to begin my brief remarks on Bill C-43 relating to abortion by saying that for all members of the House of Commons, it is a difficult decision. I hope all members will make the decision bearing in mind the interests expressed across Canada against abortion and in favour of women's choice.
It is not a decision one can make lightly. I do not accept the political ideology that we have just heard in the House of Commons from that member of the NDP and other members who put it on a basis of no decisionmaking, the decision is made. That is not true. The decision has to be made by members of the House based upon their own view of life in Canada and the social values of Canadians in their own constituencies, across the regions and throughout the country. It is not a decision to be made lightly. I want you to know, Mr. COMMONS DEBATES
May 22, 1990
Government Orders
Speaker, I have put a great deal of thought into the process.
First, I want to make clear that the decision I made for myself is that there must be a law in Canada with respect to abortion. The existing situation where we have a void as a result of the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada is not acceptable to the great majority of Canadians. I say that with respect to the views of those who believe that Canada, and life in Canada, can continue without a law on abortion. I think that is a view people hold with real emotion but, at the same time, it is not a view that I personally can accept. I want to make it clear to all my colleagues in the House of Commons that I believe there must be a law on abortion.
The difficulty is in what should be the content of that law. I think members must realize the legal parameters set down by the Supreme Court of Canada with respect to a law on abortion. It is not possible, in my opinion, for the House of Commons to enact a law that precludes abortion in all circumstances. There must be circumstances in which abortion can be performed. Any law that says otherwise would not meet the tests and the dictates of the Supreme Court of Canada, which is the lawful determining authority under the Canadian Constitution and under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
Those who believe that there ought to be a law which totally voids abortion in all circumstances will have to seek an amendment to the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. That can only be done under very special circumstances. What is at stake in relation to the Charter of Rights and Freedoms is the protection of the foetus not now recognized under the Constitution. In order to fully protect life as it exists in the foetus, there must be a constitutional amendment to the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. We are dealing with a specific bill relating to abortion law in Canada which must meet the test imposed by the Supreme Court of Canada. It is in that context that we must examine Bill C-43. It is difficult to consider the nature of an abortion law without reviewing one's own feeling in addition to the feelings of the Canadian society as represented in constituencies such as Halifax West and provinces like Nova Scotia and across the country.
In order to respond to what one perceives to be the prevalent view, I think it is difficult to accept the law imposed by Bill C-43. As has been said by so many members, it virtually includes abortion in those circumstances. The only condition would be that a medical practitioner must direct the performance of the abortion
and it must be based on health grounds of the broadest kind.
I am going to look very carefully at amendments proposed by colleagues in the House of Commons that would restrict the definition of health and would add restrictions to the law proposed by Bill C-43. If those amendments do not pass then I, as all members, will be faced with the decision of whether or not to support Bill C-43 or vote to defeat that legislative measure.
Again I repeat that I believe very strongly that we must have an abortion law in Canada. In the few moments available to me today I want to indicate why I would question the provisions of Bill C-43. May I say that I proposed an amendment to Bill C-43 in the House of Commons that would have defined medical facility as an approved hospital or medical clinic and would have required that the kind of abortion permitted under Bill C-43 be performed there.
I am very disappointed that the Chair did not see fit to permit that amendment to be included in the list of amendments relating to the abortion law because I think it is very important to Canadians, particularly in Nova Scotia and my area of Halifax. If abortions are to be performed, they must be performed under very careful circumstances. We have the requirement that a medical practitioner must be involved, but if abortion can be performed anywhere determined by the medical practitioner, that is going to create difficulties.
As is well known, Dr. Henry Morgentaler and perhaps others believed that they should be permitted to perform abortions in a clinic they have established. I am sure if that precedent is established as part of our law, many clinics will spring up across the country for the performance of abortion.
Those who believe in free choice will welcome that change. But for those who want to be extremely careful in determining the circumstances in which an abortion might be allowed, this will pose very grave difficulties. It will be unacceptable to those who oppose abortion, as well as to those who would only permit abortion under limited circumstances.
May 22, 1990

I find it very difficult to support the bill in the absence of a provision restricting the place in which abortions can be performed. In the province of Nova Scotia a law has been enacted to restrict the place in which abortions are performed. That law is now before the courts and there is great danger that if Parliament does not act to restrict the place in which abortions may be performed, provincial laws may be declared invalid once legislation such as Bill C-43 is passed.
This is a very technical legal point but it is one that is going to cause serious difficulty, not only in Halifax and Nova Scotia, but across Canada. I think if there is one thing I glean from conversations with my constituents and Canadians in other places, it is that there should be a law pertaining to abortion. That law must be carefully administered. It cannot be carefully administered unless the places at which abortions are performed are restricted.
In closing, I have the greatest sympathy for those who believe that it is a woman's right, in certain circumstances, to have an abortion. I cannot as an individual and as a member of Parliament accept that view. I do not want to increase the possibility of danger to women in the matter of child bearing. I realize that there should be other measures to avoid situations that result in unwanted pregnancies and I would support any of those measures. For the moment, my position is dear: There must be a law on abortion in Canada and that law has to be carefully crafted in order to ensure that abortions are restricted and that those restrictions are carefully monitored.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to oppose Bill C-43 and all amendments proposed thereto, with the exception of amendment No. 24, standing in the name of the hon. member for New Westminster-Burnaby.
I am not going to dwell on the legalities of the matter. It is not that they are unimportant but because I have only a few minutes. I am not going to argue about the rights of a woman versus the possible rights of the foetus, although undoubtedly that is a question that must be dealt with. I do not think the matter rests at the level of legalities. I want to deal with the underlying moral debate, the reason why some people say and sincerely
Government Orders
believe that we must have a law in the Criminal Code prohibiting and punishing abortion.
The argument, as it is most usually presented, is that abortion is the killing of a person; a person yet unborn but a person. As we have laws to prevent the killing of a person who has been bom, so we should have law to prevent the killing of a person who has not been bom. It is also said on the basis of some very particular traditions that this is contrary to the teaching that we know as God's law. I take God and his law seriously, Mr. Speaker, although I think that there is far more to God than what we call His law, such as laws that have been written down in the Bible and in other books. There is God's creation, God's forgiveness and God's love. The law is really a smaller part than those, and I will come back to that later.
The reason I do not accept the very simple argument as it is put forward is that I do not think it works. Even if I were to accept the view that the unborn is a person and that abortion is there for the killing of a person, I oppose this bill. I oppose it because it will not work. It will not stop abortions no matter how it is amended. Therefore, it causes trouble to no good end. It causes useless trouble to women and doctors.
The reason why I say it will not work is that abortions have been done since the earliest time of our history even though people in those days, as in our days, had reverence for life. It is not reasonable to get hysterical about saying our civilization must not decide to kill the unborn. The shoe is on the other foot. The question is: Have we arrived at the point in our civilization where it is possible that no one will kill the unborn? That is the challenge but it is a very different one.
Abortions have not only been performed in the past, they are performed in our own time, in Christian countries such as Ireland that have ferocious laws penalizing abortionists. There is a high rate of abortion in Ireland as there is in some other countries that are not Christian. In other words, they appeal to what people say is God's law on the matter, but the backing up of that appeal by the threat of prison does not stop abortion. That is a matter of experience and a matter of fact.
When we had punitive laws in Canada they did not stop abortion. They drove it underground. Abortions were done secretly or abroad. When they were done secretly they were often badly done. They succeeded as

May 22, 1990
Government Orders
abortions in killing the unborn but they also at times did great harm, even to the point of killing the mother.
I think a previous speaker summed it up very well when he said that the best way to protect the unborn was to protect the mother. This is assuming that the unborn is a person to which some hold and some disagree. Taken at the point of the strongest argument against abortion, namely the argument that it is a person there in the womb, the best way to protect what is in the womb, person or not, is to protect the woman carrying it.
As a practice to be legislated by us, it is simply not practically possible to protect the unborn against the will of the mother. The only way to do that would be to threaten violence on the mother, and that is bound to have a dangerous effect on the child. We can all imagine the ways in which that may happen. The threat of violence against the pregnant woman might affect the child in her womb, nevertheless the experience of threatened violence against her has not prevented the practice of abortion.
There are other things that can be done. I regret that so much attention is given by some parts of our society in Canada to the negative means, to the threat, to the use of violence either directly or as a threat. It has been pointed out many times in previous debates and again today that there are many women who choose abortion who would not choose it, who would choose to bear the child if they were given the support that would be fitting to the position of people who say we must reverence life.
I have had experience on the Toronto City Council where certain people, who spoke about reverence for life, condemned abortion and Planned Parenthood because they might sometimes give someone advice about how to procure an abortion. There was a five-hour debate about whether to give $500 to Planned Parenthood. Some members said they would not vote for it because they reverenced life.
Those same members of council despised life once it was bom because they also voted against a by-law that would stop landlords from excluding tenants on the ground that they had children. So the unborn have rights but the born have no rights; that is ridiculous. If this House, including the government side, seriously wishes to protect the unborn, it can do far more than this law could ever do. It could provide for the economic and health maintenance of the pregnant woman be she married, unmarried, rich or poor. It could provide for decent medical treatment, which to some extent our country provides better than the United States does for
its poor people. That is one reason why some of us want to keep our economy safe from the American takeover.
It could provide decent housing accommodation for the parent or parents and child. It could provide decent working conditions and could respect the work of women who still carry the huge majority of the work of raising children.
By the laws of our country there is a whole class of women expected to do the work of child raising and housekeeping who are paid rotten, low wages, who are kept in positions of semi-servitude, and who are forbidden even to try to organize a union on their behalf. We call them the immigrant domestic workers. We bring them to Canada because the pay for the work they do is so rotten and the conditions of abuse, sometimes physical or even sexual abuse, are so rotten where they work that Canadian women will not do that work. That shows how this government and this House despise the work of women, particularly the work of raising children.
Until we change that and give decent recognition to the work of raising children, we have no right to threaten violence against a pregnant woman who decides not to bear a child. Therefore, as I say, I would oppose all the amendments that are proposed today, except for Motion No. 24, standing in the name of the hon member for New Westminster-Burnaby. It would simply strike out all the sections that provide for violent penalties against the woman or doctor who take part in an abortion. It will do no good. It will do a great deal of harm. If we are serious as a House, we can do much better.

Mr. Speaker, earlier I spoke in support of my two amendments which in essence would safeguard the pregnant woman having the abortion based on genuine medical indications.
The member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell whose motion I seconded indicated that a medical procedure had only to be induced by a medical practitioner. It stands to reason that when the procedure to be done will effect the destruction of the unborn, it should be carried out wholly and solely by the physician so that he or she can assume the ultimate medical responsibility.
May 22, 1990

Were we to allow people other than physicians to perform the procedure for genuine, medical indications, first, the indications may not exist. Second, we may franchise abortion clinics across the country. Third, there can be an assembly line for doing abortions. When that happens truly the practice of medicine will be corrupted.
The amendment proposed by my colleague is an attempt to ensure that the physician truly does the procedure and does it according to medical standards.
For the last minute, I cannot help but comment on the information of the previous speaker. He indicated that we do not need this law because it will not work. That is not an argument against introducing a law. There is a law against murder, there is a law against death, and we have not eliminated those offences from this earth. Inability to eliminate offences completely is no excuse not to enact a good law.
The last speaker indicated that many women would not choose abortion if support was given to the pregnant woman so that she would be encouraged to proceed with that pregnancy to term. If that were the true answer to
Government Orders
the problem, why then propose an answer that is no answer at all?
The Supreme Court of Canada, in saying that the state has a legitimate interest to protect the life of the unborn, is telling Canadians that it is part of our rule of law enshrined in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
I object to this bill being unamended because although it is difficult to compromise the two opposing views it does not really reconcile the two at all. We cannot equate the right to choose on the part of the women versus the right to live on the part of the unborn. Only two lives may be equated, and that is why there is a need to ensure that medical indications are safeguarded and that the one who will do the procedure is a medical practitioner.
